title: Diary of the Last Gravedigger
text:
"Third week of thaw. Buried Hanne Moss, the miller's widow, in the north row. The parish pays four pennies a grave. A man in a grey coat stood by the wall the whole time, and afterwards he asked whether I nail the lids. I said I do. He gave me twelve pennies not to.
Fourth week. Four more from the fever. I left the lids loose, as he asked. I tell myself the dead feel nothing either way and twelve pennies is twelve pennies. On Sunday the grave of Hanne Moss had sunk a hand's width, the way a grave sinks when the coffin under it is empty.
Fifth week. I dug down at night to look. The coffin was there and she was not. At the foot end someone had pulled out two boards from the far side, from the direction of the old crypt wall, and the earth behind them was loose and smelled like the cellar under the abbey.
Sixth week. The man in grey came again. He asked how deep I dig. Six feet, I said. He said six feet is too shallow for what he needs, and asked whether I had a son to help me dig deeper."

title: Treatise on Cold Iron and Bone
text:
"From the shop of Brannoch, armourer to the Crypt Watch, for every man who takes the stair down.
Damp undoes more mail than any sword. Oil your rings every night with mutton tallow, not linseed, which turns sticky in the cold and holds grit. A rusted ring opens under a blow that a clean one would turn.
The footmen swing low and flat, so the cut comes in under the shield at the thigh. Wear the long mail skirt even if it chafes. The archers shoot splinters of bone ground thin, and these find the gap under the arm. I sew a gusset of doubled rings there. Do the same, or pay me to.
Lace your plates before you go down, not after. Fingers go numb by the third landing, and nobody has ever laced a vambrace properly in the dark with a wight coming at him."

title: Litany of the Hollow Monarch
text:
"Taken from a man in a grey robe arrested at the abbey wall. Copied for the bishop's file by Imre Saltash, clerk.
'Who sits below? The king who did not leave. Who keeps his oath? The bones who did not leave. What did he promise? That no man of his would rot alone. What does he ask? Eight breaths and a name. When will he rise? When the hall is full.'
My note: the man would not say which king. I searched the rolls. King Morvath had the lower vaults cut in the eleventh year of his reign, during the Long Winter, for the soldiers who died of the fever, and ordered every one of them buried with his sword. He was laid among them in ermine two winters later. The rolls say the great hall below was cut for three thousand. By my count of the parish books, some two thousand nine hundred have gone down so far."

title: Report from the East Vaults
text:
"Sergeant Ulric Dane to the Captain of the Crypt Watch, after the clearing of the east vaults.
Sir, you asked why we lost Pask and Merrit and not the men in front. The ghouls do not come at the shield line. They wait in the side niches until we pass, then go for whoever walks last, which is the lantern boy or the man carrying the wounded. Pask was carrying Merrit.
Once a man is down they stop fighting. Three of them knelt over Merrit and ate while we hacked at them, and I swear the cuts closed as they fed. When they got up they were faster than before. We killed them, but it took the whole section.
My recommendation is that the strongest man walks last, not first, and that we carry our dead out at once, before anything else, even if the vault stays half cleared. I have told the men that if I fall they are to drag me out first, and that this is an order."

title: Prioress Vespera's Confession
text:
"Father, the water in our font rises from the cistern under the lower parish, under the old graves. I have known this since my first winter as prioress. When the fever came and the bishop wrote asking for signs, I drew from the font, blessed the water and sprinkled the sick, and some of them got up. I wrote to the bishop that it was grace.
They got up, but they did not get well. They stopped eating bread. They asked the kitchen for raw meat, and two had to be tied to their beds. Sister Gerlind said the water tasted of iron and earth, so I sent her away to the hill farms to stop her saying it.
I am not asking for absolution. I am asking you to have the cistern bricked up when I am gone, because I will not do it. I have tried three times. Each time I get as far as the steps, and then I fill the bucket instead."

title: Ossuary Masonry: Volume I
text:
"Master mason Ponce to his apprentices, the first lesson of the ossuary.
A long bone is lighter than a stone of the same length, and that is why apprentices get careless with it. A wall of thighbones laid crossways and keyed with skulls every fourth course weighs more than you think by the time it reaches your chest, and you will be lifting it all day for a month.
So: feet a shoulder apart, back straight, the load close to the belly, and the push comes from the legs. Breathe out as you lift, never in. I have buried two apprentices who lifted with their backs. I set them in the north wall myself, fourth course, so the rest of you can see them while you work.
Do not take bones from the lowest bins. Those are the king's soldiers and they are counted. The Choir counts them too."

title: Eulogy for the Nameless Vanguard
text:
"Spoken by Chaplain Tobiah Crane at the memorial for the White Hawk company, written down by a novice.
'Forty-one men of the White Hawk went down the crypt stair on the feast of Saint Ilse with lanterns, rope, and the Count's promise of a pension for their widows. None came up. I cannot read you their names, because that same week the muster roll went missing from the Count's own chancery, and without a roll there are no widows on paper and no pensions to pay.
'I knew some of them. One was a farrier from Lowmere with a bad knee. Two were brothers who had lied about their age. One sang badly and often. One owed me money, and I forgive it. Their families are in this chapel and know who they were, even if the Count does not.'
The novice adds: the next morning the Count's steward asked for a copy of the sermon. The chaplain gave it to him, and within the month he was posted to the crypt garrison."

title: Urns Sealed with Grey Wax
text:
"Order of the Crypt Watch, nailed up at the head of the east gallery.
The urns in the galleries below the third landing hold the dead of the Long Winter. In the worst months the abbey could not burn bodies fast enough, and the half-burned were packed into urns with rue and sealed with grey wax.
Most hold nothing worse than ash. Some still hold the fever. In the clearing of the east gallery the men broke ninety urns, and thirteen of them gave off a yellow-grey smoke that took the skin off Corporal Fenn's throat. He breathed it for less time than it takes to say the Creed and was dead by evening.
Therefore: no breaking urns for sport or to look for rings. If one breaks, step back at once and stay out of the smoke until it settles, which takes about as long as a slow count of four. Do not go back into it to help a man. Drag him out by the feet with a hook."

title: The Fencing Master and the Dead
text:
"The dead do not feint. A living swordsman lies with his eyes and his shoulders; a skeleton has no eyes and no muscle to lie with. What it has is a hip. Before every cut the pelvis turns first, and you can hear it: a dry click, like a knuckle.
So do not watch the sword. Watch the hip, listen for the click, and step aside toward its empty hand, never back. Behind you is where the next one is standing.
I made my pupils practise blindfold against a wooden frame with real joints that Master Ponce built for me, and I rattled it from behind. The ones who laughed at the blindfold were the ones I later wrote letters about."

title: Note Under a Paladin's Gauntlet
text:
"Scratched with a buckle pin on the back of a requisition for lamp oil.
Leg broken at the pendulum corridor. The others went on to find the stair down and said they would come back for me. That was two lamp-fills ago.
I can hear chanting from the vault ahead. It goes on for a while, stops, and then something gets up and walks. I know the sound of Aldric's mail. I know Brother Hew's limp. I buried them both this morning with my own hands, properly, with the words said.
Whoever reads this: if you find a knight of the White Hawk lying here, break his bones. All of them, the skull last. If you only knock them down, they put themselves back together. I would do it myself if I could reach."

title: The Physician's Notes on the Shriek
text:
"Notes of Agnes Kell, physician to the Crypt Watch, on three men brought up from the north vaults.
All three heard the shriek at close quarters. None has a wound. Each lost his voice for a short while afterwards, about as long as it takes to draw two breaths, and could not so much as shout a warning. Brother Anselm, who was praying at the time, says the words stopped in his mouth halfway. Every torch within ten paces of the thing went out at once, though not one was knocked down.
The youngest, a cousin of the Pask who died in the east vaults, says he knew the voice. He says it was Mag Tully, who keened at his father's burial when he was a boy and was paid sixpence for it. Mag Tully died in the second year of the Long Winter while sitting vigil over the Harrow family in their vault, and the parish buried her there with them, since nobody else would take her.
I have no remedy to propose. I have written to the parish to ask where else the keening women were buried."

title: The Warm Breath: A Lesson for Novices
text:
"Learn this, then burn the page. The ghoul is honest, whatever the Watch says of it. It knows that what leaves one body must go somewhere, and so it opens its mouth. You will not eat the dead, you are not that hungry yet, but you will learn its manners.
When your blade goes in, breathe in through your teeth at that moment, not before and not after. Hold the breath while you draw the blade back and think of the warmth coming up the steel into your wrist. At first you will only feel foolish. By the hundredth cut the scratches on your own hands will close by evening, and by the thousandth you will stop counting.
Do not teach this to the Watch. They would only use it to stay down here longer."

title: Ballad of the Red Duke
text:
"From the songbook of Berthold the minstrel, with his notes.
The tavern version: when the fever came, Duke Cassian walled himself into his family vault with his household and twelve casks of red, and they sang through the Long Winter and came up in spring to a town of graves. The chorus goes 'Red wine, red Duke, red door'. Everybody knows it.
The parish book, which a clerk read to me for two pennies, says the vault was opened in the spring of the third year. Nineteen of the household lay on the shelves in good order, each with a coin on the tongue. The casks were empty. The Duke was not there. The masons who broke the door said the last course of bricks had been laid from the outside.
I still sing the tavern version. Nobody pays for the other one."

title: Notes on Tomb Moss
text:
"From the herb book of Mother Hild, apothecary at Coldharrow.
Grave moss, the blue kind that glows faintly on the lids of the old sarcophagi. Bitter, smells of almonds. A pinch chewed eases a toothache; more than a pinch brings dreams of being shut in, and few who try it want them twice. Dried and burned, it gives a light smoke that keeps flies away from a sickbed.
It grows only where something lies beneath it. The diggers know this and make use of it: a lid with moss on it is a full coffin, a bare lid is an empty one, and you need not lift it to check. Last month I went down with my basket to the north row of the lower vault. Of sixty lids, eleven were bare. I am told that in my mother's time it was two."

title: Inventory of the Valerius Vault
text:
"Inventory of the vault of House Valerius, taken for the heirs by Ivo Marten, notary.
Item: one bronze door, sound. Item: four sarcophagi of the old lords, lids cracked, contents dust. Item: two silver candlesticks, one bent. Item: one coin chest, empty, the lock forced long ago. Item: six banners, rotted past reading.
Item: three coffins of lead, soldered shut from the outside, marked on the lids in three different hands, the oldest of which I cannot read and the newest of which says 'do not'. Heavier than a body. Something inside shifts when the coffin is tilted. Not opened.
Note to the heirs: I find nothing of value here. I advise you against selling the vault to the gentleman in grey who has made you an offer, though I can give no reason that a notary could put in writing."

title: A Tomb Robber's Letter to His Nephew
text:
"So you want to go down with the crew this spring. If you must, then learn where to put the knife. The bones hold together at the neck by a peg of old gristle under the skull, and that peg goes brittle before anything else. A blade in there, angled up, and the head comes off clean. Then put your boot through the skull, or it will be up again before you have the ring off its finger. Ribs are a waste of your arm.
The ones in mail are harder. Look for where the mail has rotted at the collar and go in there, quick. Wait for the sword arm to lift. That is when the neck is open.
And take nothing from the mouths. I mean that. The coin on the tongue is the one thing down there that somebody is still counting."

title: Fragment: The First Burial
text:
"Carving on the lintel of the oldest stair, below the king's hall. Translated by Brother Wendel of the abbey, who notes that the tongue is older than the kingdom and that he is sure of perhaps half the words.
'We cut into the rock to keep our dead from the wolves and the floods. When the first room was full, we cut a second beneath it. Beneath the second we found a door that we had not cut. We closed it again. Let no one cut below this line.'
Wendel's note: the line is there, a groove a thumb wide running across the wall at the foot of the stair. The king's hall lies below it. So does everything King Morvath built."

title: Statement of the Lower Gatekeeper
text:
"Statement of Hobb Gale, keeper of the lower gate, taken before the abbey's judge.
I kept the key for nineteen years. Brass, as long as my forearm, seven pounds. I am asked why I threw it down the dry well. I will answer plainly.
Since the autumn there has been walking behind the lower door every night. Not one pair of feet. Many, back and forth, the same distance every time, like sentries on a wall. I told the prior. The prior said it was water in the pipes.
Then in Lent they started coming up to the door and standing there. I could hear them stop. The night before I threw the key away, one of them knocked three times, slowly, the way the Watch knocks when it comes back up. Nobody from the Watch had gone down that month.
The door is bowing now at the middle, outward. I have said what I know. I would like to go home."

title: Catalogue of Broken Crests
text:
"From the quartermaster's book of the Crypt Watch, western gallery.
Shields recovered: eighty. Crests: White Hawk, thirty-one; the Harrow boar, nine; the abbey key, twelve; painted over or beaten flat, twenty-eight. Fit to reissue after the smith: forty.
In the margin, in the quartermaster's hand: I have issued shields here for eleven years and I can tell you which men bring theirs back. Not the strongest. The ones who carry a full pack up and down the stair every morning whether they are going down or not, and sleep in their gambeson instead of on it. They eat their bread even when it stinks of the vault. The cold of the lower galleries gets into a tired man, and a tired man lowers his shield arm long before he drops the shield."

title: Last Rites for the Condemned
text:
"The rite read over hanged men before they are carried down to the lowest gallery, from the abbey's book of offices. The rubrics are in red in the original.
'We give you to the stone, since the earth would not have you. Lie still. Do not count the days. Do not learn the way up.'
Rubric: the body is laid face down, the hands bound behind with cord, not wire. The shroud is nailed to the shelf at its four corners. No candle is lit at the shelf, so that the dead man does not come to know the shape of a flame and go looking for it.
Added later, in another hand: since the Choir began coming down, we find the cords cut and the nails drawn. Use wire."

title: The Ratcatcher's Bait Book
text:
"Baits that still work, written down for my son Wil, who takes the licence after me. Upper drains, from the Cathedral grating to Tanner's Sluice: rendered pork fat, one part ground glass to six of fat, spread thin on a board. The rats there are ordinary and die ordinary.
Below Gate Six, under the Weir Quarter, use no glass. They smell it. Arsenic in honey worked until the spring of the flood year; then they stopped touching it, all of them in the same week, as if word had gone round. I use nothing there now but the dog and the spade.
Below Gate Nine, do not bait at all. Last month I left a tray of arsenic honey on the ledge by the old cistern and came back to find it licked clean and set neatly on my bag, with three copper pennies on top. Wil, they were Dunmark pennies, this year's mint. Something down there is paying me. I have not told the Guild, and I have not been back."

title: On the Bile of Slimes
text:
"Collect the bile of an Acid Slime only in glass or glazed clay. It goes through copper in an hour, through iron in a night, and through a glove before the man wearing it has finished swearing. Glass it leaves alone, and nobody has yet told me why.
Strike a slime and it parts into three, and each part spits weaker bile. On strips of calfskin the whole slime's bile blackened a strip in a count of nine, a part's bile in twenty-two. Less bile does not explain it. The parts lose something that is not quantity.
The Apothecaries struck me from their roll for keeping these figures. Keep yours anyway. Write down every count and every colour of the vapour. In a year you will look at a pot and know its strength before you lift the lid, and you will find that the habit does not stay at the bench."

title: The Hymn of the Green Eye, Annotated
text:
"Copied by Brother Clement, clerk to the Inquisition, from a sheet taken in the raid on the dye-works cellar. The heretics sing it at Drain Head. My notes are in brackets.
'All that falls comes down to us. All that is thrown away is given. The Eye at the bottom takes the gift and does not blink.' (The Eye is the lamp-fungus that grows over the great sump at Drain Head. It glows green and is about four paces across. We burned it on the feast of Saint Odo.)
'Feed the Eye and it will see you. Starve it and it will come looking.' (The fungus grew back in nine days, half again as large. Brother Anselm says the glow now moves across the water when someone stands at the rail, and keeps to whoever stands nearest. I have asked to be transferred to the Archives.)"

title: Casebook of a Flesh-Stitcher
text:
"Casebook, third month below. Subject: Brother Barth, ratman of the lower congregation, nine years old by his teeth. One thimble of grey serum into the great vein of the neck.
Within a quarter hour he had grown a hand's breadth at the shoulder, the skin splitting along the old stitches. He broke the chain on the table as if it were string. I struck his knee with the iron rod to test the response: no flinch, no stagger, though the knee was certainly broken. He went on walking on it.
The effect lasted while the candle burned down two fingers; then he lay down and slept for a day. The serum is skimmed from the pool beneath the Amalgam and spoils within the hour. On the days I skim it, the level of the pool rises toward the ladder, slowly, as if it were following the ladle up. Brother Aldo receives two thimbles tomorrow."

title: Krazik's Gospel of the Gutter
text:
"Written down by Ismay the copyist, who came below in the winter of the second purge. The Prophet does not write. He speaks from the back of his white beast while it feeds, and the congregation repeats each line twice so that I can keep up.
'You up there build in stone and pray for dry weather. We do not pray for weather. Every rain brings us what you dropped: your bread, your rings, your letters, your stillborn children. You throw things away and call them gone. Nothing is gone. It comes down the pipe to me, and I keep count.'
'One day the gutters will run the other way.' Here he stopped and let the beast finish eating. Nobody spoke. Then he rang the little bell on his censer once, and the rats in the walls answered all together, a sound like rain on a roof, and he said that was enough for tonight."

title: Foreman Ulm's Advice to New Flushers
text:
"You will be sick the first month. Everyone is. Do not take the Cathedral's holy water for it, it does nothing, and do not buy Brother Ansel's salve, it does worse than nothing. Do as I say instead.
Every morning a spoon of powdered charcoal in small beer and a crust of rye. Every time you come out of the sludge, find dry stone and stand on it, still, for three slow breaths before you walk on. The rot comes off you on dry stone and nowhere else. I do not know why and I do not ask.
Breathe through the nose, slowly, even when it stinks, and most of all when it stinks. By the third month your chest will be harder than those of the men upstairs who laughed at you. I have been down here twenty-two years and I have buried every one of them."

title: The Drowner's Lullaby
text:
"Report of Warden Gisla Marr, canal watch of the Weir Quarter. Since the thaw the drowned have been coming back up the overflow channels in numbers, swollen, drifting against the current. They burst when a man comes close, and where one bursts the water kills fish for a day.
Two of my men swear the drowned hum before they burst. I did not believe it until the night at Gate Four. It was a tune, low, through closed lips. Old Wenna from the laundry heard me whistling it the next morning and finished it for me. It is the river lullaby every mother in the Weir Quarter sings:
'Hush now, the water is wide, / the water is deep, / the river will carry you / home in your sleep.'
Wenna says it was her mother's. The one at Gate Four wore a laundress's apron. I have ordered the men to use the long hooks and not to go within three poles of anything floating."

title: The Tanners' Guild Ruling on Slimes
text:
"Ruling of the Tanners' Guild of Dunmark, set down after the matter of Master Corwin's cellar.
It has been the custom in Tanners' Row to keep an acid slime in a glazed tub for unhairing hides, the slime taking the hair and the fat and leaving the leather. The custom is cheaper than lime and was allowed so long as the tub was covered and the slime was fed on scraps and not let grow.
Master Corwin let his grow. When his apprentice struck it with a paddle to drive it back into the tub, it parted into three, and the three went three ways: into the drain, into the wall and into the apprentice. The cellar floor has since been found eaten through to the old sewer, and a passage of wet brick runs down from it that appears on no Water Office plan.
From this day no slime may be kept in Tanners' Row. Master Corwin is fined forty crowns, of which ten go to the apprentice's mother."

title: Engineer Grell's Letter from Prison
text:
"To whoever holds my post now. They will not let me write to the Council, so I write to you. The plans for the Low Main are in the cedar chest. Do not trust them below Gate Nine.
When we dug the Low Main we broke into a tunnel that was already there. The brick was not ours: older, smaller, fired black. The vault was too low for a man to stand, and the steps were cut for a short stride. I asked for a month to survey it. Alderman Ruel said a month cost money and told me to join the Main to it and be done, since it ran the way we wanted anyway.
It did not run where we wanted. Water we sent down it came up two streets away three days later, warm. Then the wells of the Weir Quarter began to taste of copper. When I said so in Council I was charged with embezzling lime. I have no lime. Shut Gate Nine and keep it shut, and if Ruel asks why, tell him the engineer said so from prison."

title: How the Gutter Stalkers Move
text:
"I learned this by watching the Gutter Stalkers and living, which few who watch them can say. They do not swim. They walk on the bottom, bent low, and set each foot down heel last so the silt does not cloud. Nothing on the surface moves but a little scum, and scum always moves.
Practise it in the canal at night until you can cross from Tanner's Sluice to the dye-works steps without a ripple a lantern would catch. Then practise the other half: the stillness before and the spring after. A stalker comes up all at once, from crouch to strike in the time it takes you to turn your head. Your legs will hate you for a month. After that you will move on dry land like a man carrying half his weight."

title: Deposition of a Man Swallowed and Returned
text:
"Taken before Inquisitor Pesk. The deponent is Joss Haverick, flusher of the Water Office, twenty-nine years old, burned over most of his skin as if by lime. He was swallowed by the thing in the great sump at Drain Head and spat out again when his gang struck it all at once with their picks.
He says it was not dark inside. There was a green light, and he could not breathe, and he did not die of it as quickly as he should have. He was pressed among things he names: a cartwheel, a church candlestick, a dog, a great many hands. Some of the hands still wore rings. Something closed on his arm, he says, gently, like a person trying to hold it.
He swears there was a voice he knew. Asked whose, he named Alderman Ruel, missing since the spring. Asked what it said, he answered: 'That it was warm.' The deponent has asked to go back to work. The request is refused."

title: Notice Posted at Pump House Four
text:
"Water Office. Notice to all gangs working Pump House Four and the lines below it.
The acid spouts on the Alchemists' Row line are corroded past repair and fire on their own. They keep time. Count between bursts before you pass, and pass straight after one, never just before. The spout at the bend fires on eleven, the two by the steps on seven.
The floodgate levers below Gate Six are rusted. Two men to a lever. Whoever pulls calls it out first, so that nobody is standing in the channel when the water comes.
If the mist rises above the second rung of the ladder, put out your lamp and come up by feel. Something below has learned to walk toward lamps. This notice replaces the one that told you otherwise."

title: The Leech-Woman's Teaching
text:
"The leeches the barbers buy come from the fens, and they are small and polite. The Abyssal Leech is neither. It drops from the vault onto your back, sets three rings of black teeth and drinks the strength out of you so fast that your knees give way before your blood runs short.
You will not get it off yourself, so do not try. Have your partner strike it hard and flat, with a club or the haft of an axe, and it lets go. Then do as I taught you, girl. Catch it in your fist before it reaches the water, and bite. It is full of your blood and some of the last man's. Drink yours back. Doing it, you learn that what is taken from you can be taken back, and in time your body learns it too."

title: Behind Gate Seven
text:
"Day four behind Gate Seven. The gate came down behind us when Hob pulled the wrong lever, and the lever on this side is rusted to the wall. Hob went to find a way out through the overflow on the second day. I have the lamp, half a loaf and the ledge.
The dripping from the vault keeps a pattern: four short, one long, a pause. I have listened to it for two days and it has not changed once. Water does not do that.
Day six. The lamp is out. There is a gas pocket in the corner where the bodies were dumped and I keep away from it; Hob said one spark there would take the roof off. The dripping has stopped. Instead there is a sound in the overflow pipe like wet cloth being dragged, coming closer, stopping, coming closer. Hob, if that is you, say something."

title: The Bell of Saint Gerlind
text:
"From the Cathedral inventory, year of the second purge: 'Bell of the chapel of Saint Gerlind in the Weir Quarter, bronze, fourteen hundredweight. Chapel closed for heresy. Bell to be taken down and melted for the new organ pipes.' A later hand adds: 'Bell not found. Belfry empty, ropes cut.'
Father Odran, who served Saint Gerlind's before it was closed, told the inquisitors where it went. The congregation lowered it into the drains through the old cistern under the nave, forty of them on the ropes, singing so that the street would not hear the scraping. He says it hangs now in a flooded chamber at the bottom, and the rat prophet strikes it.
He also said that when it rings a man sees his friends turn on him, and that he heard it once from the cellar steps and saw his own brother come at him with a knife, though his brother had been in the ground nine years. Father Odran was burned in the spring. The Cathedral still has no new organ pipes."

title: Apothecary's Contraband Ledger
text:
"Received at the dye-works steps, from the boatman: three crates of mole-rat distillate, sixteen vials of black lotus tincture. Paid: forty crowns, and a bottle for the watchman at Gate Four.
Sold: to Mistress Varr of the College, six vials of lotus. To the brothers of the Low Church, one crate of distillate, paid in old coin that smelled of the drains. To the gentleman in the gold coat, nothing; he only asked my prices, wrote them all down in a little book and smiled at them.
For my own use, as every evening: one drop of lotus under the tongue, held through a count of a hundred while I breathe slowly and think of an empty jar. The first weeks it burns. After that the jar grows larger. The mages pay me well because they know no cheaper way, and I do not intend to tell them."

title: The Trench Hermit's Last Words
text:
"I was called down to give the last rites to the hermit who lived in the dry niche under Tanner's Sluice. The flushers had fed him for forty years and none of them knew his name. He would not give it to me either.
He did not want absolution. He wanted to tell me something, and made me promise to write it down. 'You think the city built the drains. It did not. The drains were here, all the way down, before the first house. Your grandfathers found them and built on top, the way you build a house over a well. They fill the old channels with their muck and call them sewers.'
'Every year they go deeper than the last survey says. I have walked them. There is a stair at the bottom that is hot to the touch, and below it a light the colour of a forge.' He died before vespers. I have written it down as I promised. I do not know whom to give it to."

title: Brother Ansel's Salve, and the Coroner's Answer
text:
"A handbill pasted on the Water Office door: 'BROTHER ANSEL'S SALVE against Sewer Rot, Green Fever and Sludge-Foot. Rubbed in before going down, it hardens the skin against all filth. Two pennies the pot, at the sign of the Ladle.'
Under it, in the Coroner's hand: 'I have opened four flushers who used it. In each the skin of the legs had thickened into grey plates, like a beetle's shell, that could be lifted with a knife. Under the plates the flesh was soft and wet and had rotted unseen, because the men could not feel it. One of them had scratched through to the bone in his sleep.'
'Brother Ansel is no brother of any order I can find. The shop at the sign of the Ladle is shut. The pots are of the same glazed clay the stitchers use below.'"

title: The Rat King of Coldwell Lane
text:
"To the Aldermen of Dunmark, from the Ratcatchers' Guild. Sirs, you asked what became of the rat king found in the cellar of the Coldwell Lane bakery, which you wished to display in the Guildhall.
It was forty-one rats with their tails grown into one knot, all alive, all facing outward. Our man Hesketh carried it in a sack to the Guildhall cellar for the night. In the morning the cellar grate had been opened from below. Nothing else was taken, though the Guildhall plate was kept in the same room.
Since then our men below Gate Six report seeing it carried by the ratmen in procession, raised on a pole wound with rags, at the head of a great tide of rats. Where it is pointed, they go. We respectfully decline to recover it, and ask that the Guild's fee for the bakery cellar be paid regardless."

title: Strike Notice of the Flushers' Gangs
text:
"The gangs of Pump Houses Two, Four and Six will not go below Gate Six until the Water Office pays for two men to a lever. Three men were lost this month working the floodgates alone.
So that the men hired to break this strike do not die on their first day, here is how a rusted lever is pulled. Feet wide, the left one forward and on dry stone. Back straight. Do not pull with your arms; they will tear. Set your hands, sink, and drive up with legs and hips together, as when you lift a barrel off the ground. The rust gives all at once, so be ready to step back.
There is not a man among us who cannot lift a full barrel. Pay us, and we will show you how."

title: The Forgemaster's Bargain
text:
"I, Kasimir Pirk, notary of the Galt Works, set this down because no copy of the bargain was left to me, only what I saw. On the night the last coal barge failed to come down the river, Master Ignis called me to the casting floor to witness a sale. The buyer gave no name. It stood where the furnace light did not reach and spoke from there.
The terms were short. The fires of the Works would never again want for fuel. In return the buyer would take the two arms that served the Master best. I wrote it as I heard it and supposed it meant two journeymen bound over into service. Ignis signed. I signed beneath him.
In the morning Rolf Hult and Otto Bray, his two best strikers, came to the shift without their right arms. Taken clean at the shoulder, the stumps already healed. Neither remembered anything. By the next week the Master wore an apron with four sleeves cut into it."

title: Hedwig Sarn's Notes on Plate
text:
"From the workbook of Hedwig Sarn, armourer to the Prince's foot. The Works fluxes its iron with crushed basalt, and plate of that iron dents rather than cracks. A dent can be beaten out in the field. A crack cannot.
That is the smith's half. The wearer's half most men waste. Set every lame to overlap the one below it, so a downward cut slides off instead of lifting an edge. Keep the cuirass strap one hole looser than comfort; a tight strap carries the blow into the rib. Turn the shoulder into a stroke so it meets curved metal. Recruits learn this in an afternoon. The ones who listen come back to me for repairs."

title: Readings from Gauge Post Four
text:
"Gauge post four, east shore of the Great Melt, readings in inches against the brass mark. Morning: minus six. Noon: minus two. Evening: plus five. Night: plus nine, falling.
The lake has never kept still. Old Bernat says the mountain breathes and that is the end of it. But a mountain does not breathe four times a day, and I have kept this post long enough to set the kettle by it.
On Tuesday the reading did not fall. Plus eleven at night and plus eleven at dawn. At the second bell a row of black spines came up near the middle, each as tall as a man, and moved toward the south quay without hurry. The wave reached post four a full minute later and took the bottom rung of my ladder.
Foreman Dirk told me to write 'disturbance' in the book and nothing else. I have written it. I am also writing this, on a separate leaf, because when the reading stays high it means she is not asleep, and someone ought to know."

title: Scratched on the Wall of Flue Nine
text:
"Count of rungs, scratched with a nail on the flue wall so the next one knows. I am Tobin Marle, bound to the Works for my father's debt of forty groats, eleven years served. Yesterday the taskmaster's hook took Arno off the gantry for dropping a pair of tongs. I did not wait to be next.
Flue nine runs up from the third furnace. It is cold only on rest day, when they bank the fires, and rest day is half a day. One hundred and twelve rungs to the first bend. The imps nest at the bend. Do not touch them. When you get close they are gone, and then they are behind you, spitting. Go past with your back to the wall.
Two hundred and six rungs to the second bend. Here the soot is soft as flour and you can feel air coming down, not up. Air coming down means there is somewhere above with less fire than here."

title: The Iron Punisher's Bellows
text:
"Notes of Henning Stamm, engineer, for whoever builds the next one. The Iron Punisher has no lungs, but its hammer arm runs on a bellows, and the bellows follows a cam I cut from the swing of Bernat, the best striker the Works ever had. He could swing a twenty-pound sledge from first bell to last. He drew breath as the hammer rose and let it out as it fell, never holding it, never hurrying it.
Strikers who learned his count lasted twice as long as those who did not. So did my machines. A Punisher on Bernat's rhythm does not tire and does not stagger when struck, because nothing in it is ever out of time. Learn the count with your own chest first."

title: Vulkania's Brood Cycle
text:
"Sluice trap three, east outflow. Tally kept by Mattias Koll, sluice warden, on the Forgemaster's order. Spring: one stone, black, the size of a barrel, smooth as glass, still warm after two days in the cooling pit. Summer: none. Autumn: three, found together, one of them cracked and weeping something that set like pitch. Winter: one.
The Forgemaster wants every stone brought to him unbroken, and I do as I am told. What he does with them I do not know. The Pact men know, I think. They came to the trap one night in autumn and asked how many there had been, and wrote my answer down with the dates, as if they were counting back to something. They call them the Mother's stones.
The cracked one I did not bring. I put it in the slag trench and covered it. Two days later the crust over that spot was broken from underneath. I have asked to be moved to the west outflow."

title: The Four Hammers of Ignis
text:
"Tool store, upper forge. Issued to the Forgemaster on his order, signed for in his own hand. Hammer the first: cross-peen, thirty pounds, oak haft bound in iron, for drawing out. Returned. Hammer the second: flatter, forty pounds, for finishing. Returned.
Hammer the third: sledge, sixty pounds, the haft of solid iron and cast in one piece with the head, because no wood would hold in his grip. Not returned. Hammer the fourth: the same. Not returned.
Also issued: one pair of long pincers, the jaws lined with silver, for what he called fine work. I asked what metal needed silver jaws. He said the jaws were not for metal. Not returned.
Note: the store is to make no more hafts for the Forgemaster. I went up to the forge to ask after the third and fourth and saw why. He had set both heads on his lower pair of forearms, and the metal of him had closed over them."

title: Standing Order on Ash Imps
text:
"Standing order of the Works quartermaster, to be read aloud at every change of shift.
One. No bread, flour, lard or lamp oil within ten paces of a flue mouth. Ash imps come down for fat, not for warmth; they have warmth enough. Two. An imp is put out with sand. Water does not drown them, and the steam has scalded four men this season. Three. Do not try to catch one by hand. When you are near enough to touch it, it is no longer there, and it will be somewhere with a clear throw at your back. Corner it with two men and a sand shovel each.
Four. What an imp spits burns on bare stone for as long as it takes to say the Creed. Do not stand in it to finish a job.
Five. The reward of one groat per imp tail is withdrawn. It has come to the quartermaster's notice that the strikers of the night shift have begun breeding them."

title: The Glyph-Writer's Count
text:
"I wrote glyphs for the Pact for six years. I will not teach the glyphs, only what they taught me, which is how to hold.
A magma glyph is drawn twice: once on the stone, in the mind, line by line, and once in the stone, when you let it go. Between the two the whole figure must stay complete in your head while you count to two and a half. Lose one line and it goes off under you instead of under them.
So we drilled with nothing. The master chalked a figure, wiped it away, and made us redraw it after a hundred breaths, then after a thousand. A mind that can hold a burning figure whole while a man runs at you can hold anything you put in it."

title: The Treadwheel of Forge Three
text:
"Forge Three is blown by a treadwheel, not by water, because there is no water this deep. Twelve walk the wheel, six on and six resting, four hours to a turn. If the wheel stops, the forge loses its heat in the time it takes to boil an egg, and the Forgemaster loses a casting.
The wheel was built by the lowest bidder. On the ninth of the month the axle seized, and the six inside could not get out before the flame blew back through the forge door. Tally for that turn: six names, all struck through.
The wheel was repaired and a new gang put on it. The new gang complains that the wheel starts turning before they step in, and that something walks the inside rim beside them, keeping pace, bright enough to see by. I went to look. There is a scorched track worn into the inside rim, as from six pairs of feet. I have ordered the rim planed and the track sanded out before the next turn."

title: Operating Manual: The Soul Crucible
text:
"Procedure for the white crucible, Forge One. For the crucible crew only.
1. The charge is brought down by the taskmasters at the half bell. Do not speak to the charge. Do not ask its trade or its name, and if it offers either, do not write them down. The Forgemaster has been clear that a named charge pours badly. 2. Close the viewing shutter before the charge enters the bath. What comes off the surface in the first moment is not light, and amber glass does not stop it. Crewman Lutz looked. He is now kept in the dark room and fed by his sister.
3. When the pour runs grey, it is good soul-iron. When it runs with a blue skin, part of the charge has not let go. Skim the skin into the side mould and set it aside. Do not melt it again. The side moulds go to the Pact men, who pay for them.
4. Never pour on rest day."

title: The Chit-Runner's Trot
text:
"I carried chits between the forges for nine years and never burned a foot. The trick is no secret; nobody bothers with it.
Never stand. A grate over the melt takes your weight for about as long as it takes to say 'one'. Say it and be off. Hot plate the same: boot leather lasts a breath on it, not two. Cross the Works on the balls of your feet, short quick steps, knees soft, as over a frozen pond in spring, and look three steps ahead for the next cold place before you leave the one you are on.
Your feet learn it in a week. After a month you trot everywhere, even at home, and your wife asks what you are running from."

title: The Taskmaster's Table of Brands
text:
"Brands of the Works, as the taskmasters are to give them. A brand is set with the hot end of the hook on the back of the left hand, where a man sees it while he works.
One bar: short weight on a shift. Two bars: a tool dropped into the melt. A ring: sleeping on shift. A ring with a bar through it: speaking against the Forgemaster. A cross: a second attempt at the flues. There is no mark for a third attempt.
Found written under the copy nailed up in the barracks, in another hand: Saul Mertz has nine bars and a ring and still makes weight every shift."

title: Register of the Slag Trench
text:
"Register of the slag trench, kept by the second clerk. The dead of the Works are given to the trench at the end of each shift and entered here by name. Third week: eleven. Fourth week: nine. Fifth week: fourteen, the furnace accident.
The bodies go in, the slag closes, nothing comes back. That has been the way of it for as long as this register has been kept. I mention it only because the night watch has begun reporting lights crossing the trench toward the barracks, walking the gantries the dead used to work, passing through walls where there is no door. The watch is told to keep out of their way. Where they pass, the floor goes on burning for a while, so the watch goes round.
I have counted the lights. In the fifth week there were fourteen. I asked the first clerk whether we should keep entering the names. He says we should, so that we know who they are."

title: The Strikers' Song
text:
"Song of the upper forge strikers, for keeping time with the smith: Watch the colour, not the hand, / cherry red will bend and stand, / straw will crack and blue will ring, / strike the pale and feel it sing.
The old strikers learn what it means. A bar at heat is never one colour. There is always a paler patch where the metal is thinner or the fire caught it harder, and a blow there does the work of three. In time they stop watching the smith's hand and watch the iron, and their hammer is on the patch before the smith points.
A man in armour is never one colour either."

title: Kennel Book of the Brimstone Hounds
text:
"Kennel book, lower yard, kept by Wat Ostler, houndsman. Feed at the first and fourth bell. Scrap plate only, the thinner the better; they will not touch meat and have never needed it. A hound will eat a breastplate in a day if you let it, and its breath after is worse.
Never stand in front of one that is breathing slowly. A slow breath is drawn for the cone, and the cone burns a man's armour more than the man. Three breaths take the temper out of plate. Men of the gantry crew have walked away from a hound without a single burn and their mail falling off them like wet cloth.
They leap before they bite. If one crouches, put a wall between you, not distance; they clear twenty feet without a run-up.
The Forgemaster has asked for forty more for the upper levels by spring. I have put in for a second houndsman and twelve barrows of scrap a week."

title: Grate Inspection Rota
text:
"Rota for the inspection of grates over the melt, west hall. Every grate is to be walked by the inspector at the start of each shift and its pins tapped with the mallet. A sound pin rings. A soft pin thuds. A grate with one soft pin is chalked and closed. A grate with two is taken down.
The grates were cast to carry a loaded barrow across without stopping. They were never meant to be stood on. A man who stops on one to talk or tie his boot puts his whole weight on four pins already half soft from below, and the grate goes out from under him faster than he can cry out. The melt shows through the hole for a long while after, until somebody hangs a new grate.
Inspector's note: of the forty grates in the west hall, thirty-one were chalked this morning. I have been told to rub out the chalk and sign the rota. I have rubbed it out, and left the rota unsigned on the clerk's desk with the count written on the back."

title: The Crucible Yoke
text:
"How Mother Wilma taught the yoke crews of the casting floor to carry the crucible. A full crucible is three hundredweight of metal slung between two yokes on four shoulders, and a spilled cupful costs a foot. So nobody carries it with the arms. The arms only steady it. The lift comes up through the heels and the thighs, and the back stays a plank from neck to tailbone, because a back that bends under that weight bends once.
For a month Wilma made new crews carry a pot of sand round the floor before every shift, one shovel more each day, and never let one of them cheat a step. By the end of the year her crews could lift a cart off a man's legs."

title: The Smelter's Cough
text:
"To the Guild of Barber-Surgeons at Galt Town, from Ewald Stray, sent down to the Works at the Prince's charge to see to the lower shifts. Masters, you asked for a report on the cough. It begins as a dry tickle in the first year. By the fifth a man brings up black, and if you smear it on a white plate it glitters, which is the iron. By the tenth he cannot climb the flue ladders and is moved to the cauldron hall, where the lead fumes finish him inside a season. I have opened four. The lungs are grey and heavy as wet felt, and they sink in a bucket.
I asked the Forgemaster for wet cloths over the mouths of the furnace crews, and for one rest day in seven instead of one in fourteen. He asked how many days the cloths would add to a man. I said perhaps two years. He said the Works does not keep a man two years longer; it keeps the next man.
I had meant to come home at midsummer. The taskmasters tell me the road up is closed for repairs and the Works has need of a surgeon. I am to have rooms by the casting floor."

title: Farewell Letter from Foreman Dirk
text:
"Greta, they have closed the lower gate behind the night shift and I do not think it will open before morning, so I am writing this and giving it to the lift boy, who goes up at the change.
The melt rose two feet in the night. Sluices nine and ten are warped and will not lift. There are three vents in the roof of the casting floor that would take the heat off in an hour, and the Forgemaster will not have them opened, because he is pouring something in the great mould and a draught would spoil the cooling. He has been pouring for six days. Nobody has been told what it is. It is longer than the hall is wide, and they have had to cut into the wall.
The money is under the hearthstone, the loose one by the bellows. Give Lotte her grandmother's ring when she is twelve and not before. Do not let our Bram come down here for the wages, whatever they offer him.
The floor is warm through my boots as I write. The men are singing to keep their spirits up. I will try to send another with the lift boy tomorrow. Dirk."

title: The Astrologer's Night Log
text:
"Ninth night of the dry month. The orrery in the round chamber has eleven spheres, as it had when I took the post. Wound it at the second bell and logged the positions against the painted ceiling. All in agreement.
Twelfth night. Eleven spheres, but the outermost brass arm has a fresh scratch, as if something had been fitted to it and taken off again. Asked the night porter. He says nobody goes in but me.
Nineteenth night. Twelve spheres. The new one is glass, the size of a plum, with sand inside that does not settle. It rides on an arm I did not know the orrery had. I have not wound the mechanism since, and the spheres are still turning.
Twentieth night. I measured the track of the glass sphere. It comes a little closer each turn, toward the chair where I sit to write. I have moved the chair. - B. Swale"

title: Principles of Astral Mirroring
text:
"Copying by mirror is slower than copying by hand for the first year and faster for every year after. Stand the page before the astral glass and look at the reflection, never at the page. Hold the reflection in your head until you can read it with your eyes shut. Only then write.
Novices hate this. They are made to hold one line, then a paragraph, then a full leaf of the Concordance, forty-two lines in a small hand. By her third winter a good copyist carries whole folios behind her eyes, and her head aches less than it did when she held one line.
Do not look into the glass after the candles are put out. The Chapter asks this of everyone in the Archives, copyist or not. - Mistress of Copyists, rule nine"

title: Report on the Dissection of a Lectern
text:
"Specimen taken in the Third Gallery after it closed on the wrist of reader Jorunn Pell, who has since lost the hand. An oak lectern, ordinary to the eye, with a brass rail for the book chain. Two wardens held the lid open with pikes while I worked.
The jaws are leaves of vellum folded over and over until the edge is harder than horn, set in rows like the gills of a mushroom. A clear gum coats them. A smear of it on my own tongue took my voice for most of an hour, which explains why the readers it takes never call out.
Contents of the cavity: a brass book clasp, a ring with the crest scraped off, two fingers (not Pell's, and much older), a candle stub, and a torn leaf of the readers' register. There are eleven names on the leaf, in eleven hands. The last one is mine, in my own hand. I have never signed the register of the Third Gallery. - Odo Lacke, surgeon to the Archives"

title: The Stolen Seconds
text:
"To the Chapter, from the Clerk of Hours, in the matter of the water clocks.
Clock four, which stands by the sealed door of the east wing, loses a quarter of an hour every night. I have changed the bowl, the float and the jet. I have checked it against the sand glasses and against the cathedral bell we hear down the shaft at noon. Clock four is sound. The time goes missing on that side of the room.
Readers who sit at the east tables leave tired and quiet. Brother Tamas sat there through the winter, and in spring he could not tell me the name of his village, though he could still recite the Concordance from memory. Whatever is behind that door leaves a man what he has learned and takes his hours, with whatever happened in them.
I ask the Chapter again to move the east tables. Last time I was told that the Grand Archivist prefers his copyists to sit there, and that the matter is closed."

title: The Second Chair
text:
"Copyists of the long hall work in pairs. The reader sits on the left and reads in a low voice; the writer sits on the right and writes. A cord of plaited silk runs from his wrist to hers, so that neither can leave the desk without the other knowing. It was meant as a courtesy. A pair that rises together does not lose its place.
Ansel read for me for nineteen years. He died at the desk in the dry month, and the wardens cut the cord and carried him out. No new reader has been assigned to me. I still copy.
I can still feel the cord. When I reach the bottom of a leaf it tightens, the way it did when Ansel wanted me to wait. When I am slow it pulls, my arm goes weak, and the next letters come out in a hand that is not mine. My ink ran out in the autumn. The Chapter has not sent more, and I have not asked. - W. Hask, desk forty, long hall"

title: Notes on the Pull of Rifts
text:
"The rifts in the lower galleries do not pull evenly. Stand at the chalk line with a rope round your waist and you will feel it: a long draw, then a slack of perhaps half a breath, then the draw again, as if something on the other side were hauling hand over hand.
A warden who learns to move in the slack can walk past a rift that has swallowed carts. The drill is plain. A partner holds the rope. You face the rift and take one step sideways each time the draw slackens, never during it. In a month the timing lives in your feet and you stop thinking about it, and that is when it starts to work against blades and claws as well.
We lost Gaspard Venn learning this. He stepped on the draw. The rope came back to us cut clean."

title: Catalogue of Forbidden Shelves
text:
"Restricted wing, bay 44. Inventory taken by Archivist R. Oake.
44-A. Herbals and poisons. Complete. To be read only in pairs. 44-B. Sermons of the condemned parishes, confiscated. Complete. Several volumes are damp, though the bay is dry; do not shelve them next to paper. 44-C. Confessions taken under question, bound in calf. Two missing. The chains on both are intact and still locked.
44-D. Empty since the inventory before last. The shelf bows under a load that nothing on it accounts for, and the boards are warm to the touch.
(In a second hand) 44-D is not empty. Warden Dace was sent to clear it on the morning of the fourth and has not reported back. (In a third hand) Strike this page from the catalogue. By order of the Grand Archivist."

title: The Gargoyle's Vigil
text:
"Work order for the reading rooms, ninth year of the present Grand Archivist. Item: twenty-four seated figures in grey limestone, to be set on the shelf tops, one to each bay. Item: each to be cut with its head bowed toward the tables. Item: no figure to be cut with an open mouth.
Paid on delivery: one hundred and twenty crowns. Withheld: forty crowns, on the following complaint. The figures were set facing the tables. At the next inspection six of them faced the aisles. At the one after, one sat two bays from its plinth, over the desk of a student who had been warming his hands at a small flame against the rules. He was found underneath it.
The mason, Gerolt Fisk, says his figures do not move, and that the Archives may keep the forty crowns and hire someone else to climb up and turn them back.
(Margin, in the Grand Archivist's hand) Pay Fisk. They are doing what they were bought for."

title: The Inscription over the Inner Gate
text:
"Every novice reads the inscription over the inner gate each morning, aloud and in one breath. It is longer than it looks. Most of them run out of air before the word for 'shelf' and have to start again while the others wait.
That is the whole exercise. Lungs and mana fill and empty by the same rule: you hold more if you take it in slowly and spend it last. A novice who can read the gate in one breath by midwinter holds a ward a third longer than one who cannot, and no one has yet explained why to my satisfaction.
Read it to the end. Do not cut the last line short because your chest hurts. The last line does the work. - Mistress of Novices"

title: Malazar's Mirror Mask
text:
"Fenwick Laud, mirror-grinder, to his brother in the guild. You asked about the commission. The Grand Archivist sent his measurements on a card instead of sitting for them. I was to make a mask of astral glass, silvered inside and out, with no holes for the eyes and none for the mouth. I said he would see nothing through it. His clerk said that was understood.
I took it to him myself. He would not let me watch him put it on. When he turned round, I saw myself in it: my own face, but older than I am and thinner, and I could not look away until the clerk took me by the elbow.
He paid in full and ordered a second, smaller one, 'for later'. I have not started it. I go to the window more often than I used to and check my reflection in the pane. So far it is still my face as it is now."

title: The Surveyor's Unfinished Plan
text:
"Survey of the library grid, sheet eleven. Pace: my own, thirty-one inches. Lantern: one. Assistant: Tobi Garn, holding the chain.
The plan will not close. I walk four bays north, four east, four south and four west, and I am not where I began. I am one bay further on, at a shelf I have not marked. Each time I walk the square, the error grows by another bay.
The revolving shelves are part of it. There are more of them than the Chapter lists. Some turn when pushed, some when a particular book is drawn, and one turned by itself while Tobi was leaning on it. I felt the chain run out through my hands. When I pushed the shelf round again, there was only the back of an ordinary bookcase, and the chain lying on the floor in neat loops, the way Tobi always left it at the end of a day.
I will finish the sheet. The Chapter has paid for twelve."

title: Case Notes on Brother Tamas
text:
"Patient: Brother Tamas, copyist, forty-four years old. Brought by the Clerk of Hours, who insists the cause is a draught from the east wing.
First visit. Cannot name his village or his mother. Recites the opening of the Concordance without a fault. Asked what he did last week, he describes the work but not the days: he knows that he copied, not that he was there.
Third visit. Has lost the taste of salt. Has lost his fear of fire; he burned his palm on the brazier while I watched and only looked at it. On my advice he writes his name on the inside of his wrist every morning.
Fifth visit. The name on his wrist is written correctly. He asked me whose it was. Sixth visit. His cell was empty and the bed made. On the desk lay a fair copy of the Concordance, complete, with a blank space at the end where the copyist signs."

title: The Glyph-Cutter's Primer
text:
"Every stone has a line it wants to break along. A cutter who does not find it before the first blow ruins the slab; one who does can split a block the size of a cart with a tap. Before you cut a single rune, find the line. Wet the face and watch which way it dries. Tap along it with the back of the chisel and listen for the note that goes dull.
The glyphs in the reading room floors were cut by people who knew this, which is why they last. The habit carries beyond stone. Look at a shield, a joint, a man in armour, before you strike. Somewhere there is a seam he has not thought about. - Sixth lesson of the Guild of Cutters"

title: Notice Pinned to the Reading Room Door
text:
"NOTICE, by order of the Warden of the Reading Rooms.
One. Readers will not break or lean on the furniture of the upper galleries. When a table or shelf breaks, the books on the nearest shelves wake. No one has determined why. They leave the shelf at the height of a man's head, and they do not stop for a closed door.
Two. A book that has left its shelf is not to be caught. Reader Hollis caught one in the last week of autumn and it opened in his hands.
Three. The cost of repairing furniture will be taken from the reader's deposit. The cost of repairing a reader is a matter for his family."

title: The Instrument-Maker's Letter
text:
"Mistress Selk, I have your astrolabe back and can find no fault in it. The rings are true, the alidade turns freely, and on my bench it tells the hour to the minute.
You write that in certain rooms of your library the needle swings and will not settle, and that in the same rooms your wardens find a ward costs them half again its usual strength one day and half its usual strength the next. I have no explanation for the second. As for the first, a needle behaves like that near lodestone or near a great mass in motion, and I would not stand long in a room whose floor is not lodestone.
I have marked the rooms on your plan as you described them. Laid out together, they make a line that runs from the round chamber with the orrery to the sealed east wing. You will know better than I do what that means. I return the plan with my bill, and I ask you not to send for me again. - Aurel Penn, instrument-maker"

title: The Memory House Drill
text:
"In her first month every novice builds a house in her head, with the doors exactly where they were in the house she grew up in. In the front room she puts her own name. In the kitchen, her mother's name. By the hearth, the face of the first person she saw die. In the cellar, one thing she has never told anyone.
Every morning she walks through the house before she opens a book. If a room is empty, she tells the Mistress of Novices and does not go to the east tables that day.
The house is also where she keeps what she reads, and a copyist who walks it daily remembers six times as much as one who does not. The Chapter says that is why the drill is taught. The other reason is explained only after the oath."

title: The Inkmaker's Ledger
text:
"Ink for the long hall, made monthly. Oak galls, eight pounds, crushed. Green vitriol, two pounds. Gum, one pound. Rainwater, four gallons. Steep nine days in the copper vat, stir daily.
From the spring of the fifth year, by order of the Grand Archivist, the rainwater was replaced with water drawn beside the rift in the lower gallery. The ink came out blacker and dried in half the time, and the copyists said it was the best they had ever had.
Ninth month. Vat down three inches overnight. Lid on, no leak. Tenth month. Down a foot, and the stirring paddle gone. A black trail a hand wide runs from the vat to the drain, still wet. I followed it to the drain and stopped there.
Eleventh month. Vat empty, lid still on. I have asked for a new vat and a second lamp for the cellar."

title: The Echo of the Unwritten
text:
"We went into the Archives four. I want that written down before anything else: four. Myself, Brother Halvard with his mace, Ottilie with the bow, and young Teodor Wick, who did fire. We had been four since the Crypt.
In the reading room past the round chamber we were five. Nobody saw the fifth come in. There were two of Ottilie, the same bow and the same burn on the same cheek, and both of them looked at us as if we were the ones who had gone mad. One of them asked Halvard about his sister, by name.
Halvard said the false one would cast no shadow. They both cast one. In the end he asked each of them what we had eaten in the Sewers. One of them told him. The other said she did not know, and drew.
I do not know if we killed the right one. Ottilie has been very quiet since. She shoots as well as she ever did."

title: The Binder's Method
text:
"From the binder's book of the long hall, for apprentices. A cover that is to last in these rooms must be boiled. Soak the hide a full day in cold water. Lower it into water just short of the boil and lift it out the moment it darkens and draws in; a breath too long and it turns brittle. Shape it over the boards while it is soft, dry it slowly by a low fire, and rub in beeswax and alum until it will take no more.
The wardens came to us for this when their jerkins kept splitting on the pikes in the Third Gallery. A jerkin done this way turns a blade that would open a plain one. Apprentices learn it on book covers first, because a spoiled cover costs the Archives less than a spoiled warden."

title: The Last Entry in the Grand Index
text:
"The Grand Index is kept in one hand at a time. I took it over from Archivist Oake in my thirtieth year, and the last entry in his hand is a herbal received from the Kurgan parishes.
After it come three entries I did not write. The hand is like mine, but slower. 'Swale, B. Night log of the round chamber. Incomplete. Shelved: east wing.' Swale was the astrologer. He was not seen after the twentieth night of the dry month, and the entry is dated the twenty-first. 'Tamas, Br. The Concordance, fair copy. Unsigned. Shelved: east wing.'
The third entry is the shortest. It gives this page by its number, my name as its author, today's date, and the same shelf. I have locked the Index in the warden's chest and given him the key."

title: A Forester's Report on the Black Oaks
text:
"To the steward of Haske Hall, from Abel Corran, forester of the north edge. As ordered, we felled four of the black oaks below the mounds for the new palisade. The first one bled when the axe went in. Not sap, sir. It ran red, it clotted on the blade, and the men would not go on until I took the axe myself.
We dug around the roots of the second to learn what feeds them. At four feet we found jawbones laid in rows like cobbles, a hundred or more, and a root threaded through every one.
The stakes have stood a month now. Each morning there is a dark wet ring at the foot of every stake, though it has not rained since the hay was in. The hounds lick it and grow fat. A man who cut his hand on the bark has a wound that will not close while he works near the fence.
I ask leave to burn the stakes and pay the men off. Two of them will not come back for any wage."

title: Rite of the Stag-Bearers
text:
"For the autumn rite, as the priests of the Antlered Lord kept it before the blight.
Before a boy may wear antlers he carries the slain stag from the ford to the high dolmen on his own shoulders, nine hundred paces, all of them uphill. He may not set it down. If he does, the stag is opened where it fell and left to the crows, and he goes back to the ford for the next one.
Teach him to carry with the bones and not the arms. The spine stands like a driven stake, the knees stay soft, the weight lies across the neck and both shoulders at once. He breathes out on every left step and on every right he sings the short verse: 'Bone for bone, the Lord is fed.' By his third autumn he carries the stag and the boy who failed.
In those years the Lord drank venison. Write that down plainly."

title: Lady Isolde's Wedding Gift
text:
"Dearest Maud, the house is cold and the margrave is kind, which is more than you promised me. On the morning after the wedding Ruprecht gave me pearls, twelve of them, grey as a dove's breast. He says they came out of the black water under the old mounds, where no oyster has ever lived, and that his mother wore them, and her mother before her.
They are warm when I take them off at night, warmer than my skin. Last night I laid them in the jewel box, and this morning there were eleven, and in the silk lining a small round hole the size of a pea. My maid swears on her children that she touched nothing. Ruprecht laughed and said the mounds always take back a little of what they give.
I have counted them again while writing this. Eleven. I have not told him that my throat itches, or that at night I hear something in the walls of the weaving room, like a spindle turning."

title: Hob Wennick's Advice on Snares
text:
"For whoever has my snares after me. Hob Wennick.
The roots on the mounds close on a foot in the time it takes to say your name, and every thorn on them points back toward the earth, like a fish hook. Pull straight up and you tear the leg open to the bone. I have seen it done.
Turn the foot instead, toe first, the way the root curls, as you would ease off a wet boot. The hip does it, not the ankle. Let the knee go loose and the leg comes round on its own. I made my boy walk through a blackthorn hedge every evening until he could pass without a scratch. It took him one summer and most of his shirts.
And never step where the earth has just been turned. When there is fighting on the mounds, that is where the thorns come up."

title: The Barrow Hag's Broth
text:
"Deposition of Hanne Tollis, of Karr, taken by the reeve two days after the autumn fair.
The witness says that the woman from the barrows came at dusk, when her son Jory had lain three days in the fever. She asked no payment. She asked for a pot, a bunch of nettles, a fistful of earth from the churchyard, and the mother's left hand. She cut the palm and let it run into the broth until the witness grew faint, then fed the broth to the boy with a horn spoon. By morning the fever had broken.
Since then the witness has lost flesh, so that her rings slip from her fingers, and her hair comes out in the comb. The boy is fat and has not been sick a day. Asked whether she would let the woman in again, the witness said yes, if it were for Jory.
The reeve notes that the witness is twenty-six years old. He would have put her at sixty."

title: Anatomy of the Rotwood Treant
text:
"Field notes of Dunstan Pell, sapper sergeant, on the thing we felled at the third mound.
Six men with felling axes, two days. It does not give when struck. The roots hold it like a tent peg, and a ram would break before it moved. When it slams the ground, a row of sharpened stakes comes up in front of it, straight as a hedge and some twenty paces long. Stand to the side of it, never in front.
The heartwood is hollow. The tree grew up through the roof of a burial chamber: horse bones, a bronze cauldron with Foundry marks on the rim, and a man in a fur cloak sitting upright, the root grown in through his mouth and out at the back of his skull. The cloak was still dry.
Do not use fire. Captain Hale's men tried it last year, and it walked into their tents burning.
This morning the stump has new shoots. They lean toward the camp."

title: The Crimson Dolmen
text:
"My grandmother sat the vigil under the red stone when she was twelve, the year the last stag was offered. She taught it to me, and I write it down so it is not lost with me.
From dusk until the sun touches the capstone: no fire, no cloak, and no food since the day before. Do not fight the cold. Let it in as far as the skin and hold it there. Breathe in through the nose for four, hold for four, and let it out through the mouth so slowly that it warms your chest on the way. Every hundred breaths, stand, stamp, and sit down again.
Never lean back against the stone. It drinks heat and gives none back. In the old days those who fell asleep against it were laid under the next stone in spring.
Those who came down in the morning could march two days on one meal."

title: A Barber's Casebook
text:
"From the casebook of Lenz Aubry, barber to the Kurgan company.
After the fight at the eastern ring I drew forty-one red ticks out of the men's ankles and calves. Most had burst already. The rest come out whole if you twist them to the left with hot tongs. They are fat with blood, and on the underside they have something like a face, two eyes and a wet mouth, too much like an infant's. Crushed, they scream, and within the hour we hear hounds, though no one in this company keeps dogs.
They hatch in the pools of blood the dead leave behind. The sergeant now has every pool salted and covered with turf after a skirmish.
I keep one alive in a stoppered jar and feed it a drop of my own blood each night. Whichever way I turn the jar, it crawls to the south side of the glass. South of here there is nothing but the deep mounds and the old silk-house of the margraves."

title: Diary of a Lost Woodsman
text:
"Second day. Fog since dawn. My torch lights three paces, where in the yard at home it lit ten. I blaze every tree I pass, low on the left, as my father taught me.
Third day. Turned back to follow my blazes home. The marks are gone.
Fourth day. Found blazes again and followed them. They lead downhill, toward the mounds. They are mine; I know my own stroke, two cuts, the second one slanting. But the sap still runs out of them red and warm, and I have not cut a tree since yesterday noon.
Fifth day. Hounds all night. The axe is not where I left it."

title: The Covenant of the Hungry Winter
text:
"We, the eleven of Captain Ostrow's company who lived to see the thaw among the mounds, set this down and put our marks to it.
First. We drink only from what we have killed with our own hands, and only while it is warm. We learned it from the dead: they stand in the blood pools and their wounds close. A man who opens the vein of what he has just killed and puts his mouth to it gets the same mending, if he does it at once. Brother Haim showed us that in the second week. It is how we lasted.
Second. No one of us will say where Brother Haim is buried, or why there is no grave.
Marks: Ostrow, Lisk, Dobbe, both Lunds, Mattis, Cole, Pegg the Younger, Sander, Udo, and the cross of Jens, who cannot write."

title: What the Marsh Light Took
text:
"To the Keeper of the Lower Stacks, from Adept Teodora Kell, on loan to the Kurgan company. You asked for an account of the lights the men call will-o'-the-blights. Here it is, with a request that you send another adept before the new moon.
It came out of the fog in the second watch, a pale orb no bigger than a fist, drifting the way a moth drifts. I was holding a full ward for the morning behind the breastbone, as we are taught. When the thing came within ten paces I went blind, and I felt the ward run out of me like water from a cracked jug, all of it, in two breaths. Then the light burst and the ward came back as a blow. It broke Corporal Fenwick's arm and two of my ribs.
It drinks what you carry and throws it back at you. The fighting men lose their battle-fury to it the same way. Keep your reserves low near the bog, or keep away from it."

title: Item Forty-One
text:
"From the stock book of Archibald the Gilded.
Item forty-one. Helm made from the skull of an eight-point stag, antlers whole, lined with felt. Bought from a party coming up out of the Kurgan for nine gold, which was too much.
Sold the same week for thirty. Returned within the month: the buyer had stopped eating cooked meat and woke every night standing barefoot at the tree line. Refunded half. Sold again for twenty. Returned with the same complaint, and the buyer's wife reports moss growing in his bootprints. Refunded half. Sold for twelve to a gentleman who said he did not believe in such things. Not returned. The gentleman has not been seen since the first frost.
Last night item forty-one came back into the vault by itself. The lock was not touched. Price lowered to six. It is not to be kept inside overnight."

title: Harvest Roll of Hollin Ford
text:
"Harvest roll of Hollin Ford, kept by the reeve.
First year after the high dolmen was left unfed: forty bushels from the long field. Good grain. Second year: twenty-six bushels. The ears are black at the tip. The miller says the stones run wet when he grinds it and the flour comes out pink. The bread smells of tallow; the pigs eat it, the children will not.
Third year: eleven bushels. Two cows dead in the low pasture with their mouths full of thorn. Martje Hollis was delivered of a girl whose fingers are as hard as twigs. The child is healthy and does not cry.
At the meeting this evening the elders voted to feed the high dolmen again at midsummer, as was done before the margrave's father forbade it. My objection is recorded. They have not said what they will lay on the stone, and nobody looked at me while they voted. My daughter turns fourteen at midsummer."

title: Four Days Watching a Bramble Warden
text:
"I lay four days in the brambles below the third mound to watch one Warden at its work. Here is what I learned. It has kept me alive since.
It never shoots at a man who is walking. It waits for him to stop, to drink, to look at a map, to turn and call to the man behind him. A man who has stopped will not move for three heartbeats.
It does not aim at the chest. It aims where the armour has to bend: the hollow under the arm, the back of the knee, the gap above the collar. One javelin there is worth five in a breastplate. And it looses on the out-breath, when the body is quietest.
I have hunted that way ever since, deer and men alike. I have also had a smith close the gap above my own collar."

title: The Weeping Dolmen of Karr
text:
"Brother Tam Ivers to the Chapter, from the village of Karr.
The stone weeps as reported. On the morning after the solstice clear water runs from the underside of the capstone for about an hour, and the villagers catch it in clay cups. It smells of lilac. I tasted it: salt and iron, like a nosebleed. The water does heal. Old Gesche's cataract is gone. She now spends her days staring at the ground at her feet and will not say what she sees there.
The villagers say the stone weeps only in years when it has been given something the night before. When I asked what, the headman said the Chapter would not want to know.
They have been very kind to me and want me to stay for next year's weeping. Today the headman's wife asked whether I had any family who would come looking for me, and wrote down my answer."

title: Accounts of the Weaving Room
text:
"Household accounts of Haske Hall, the weaving room, kept by the steward.
Paid to the four weaving women for six ells of mound-silk, spun from the cocoons brought up from under the north barrow: two gold. Lamp oil for the weaving room: twice the usual. The women say the work must be done at night, when the spools are fullest.
For the Lady's new gown, measurements taken by the head weaver. Grey silk, no seams. The head weaver reports that the spools are heavier in the morning than when they were set down at night. No explanation given.
The Lady has not come out of the weaving room in nine days. Her meals are taken in and come out eaten. The women say the gown is nearly finished, and that the Lady has asked to be fitted while she sleeps.
The margrave orders the door kept bolted and asks that the oil be left off these accounts from now on."

title: Rules of the Mound Diggers
