text:
"Rules of the diggers of Brenn's Cross, as Old Fenn gave them to us.
One. Before the spade goes in, drive an ash stake through the turf to the depth of your arm. If it comes up wet and red, fill the hole and walk away. Two. Never dig a mound with a stone at its head. Three. Take the bronze, leave the coin in the mouth. Four. Do not cut a root you find in a grave. Go round it. Five. If you hear hounds and none of us keeps hounds, leave the tools and run. Six. A tenth to Fenn.
Added below, in another hand: Fenn broke the fourth rule at the long mound by the ford. The root closed on him before we could pull him out. We filled the grave in over him as he was. We did not stake him, and we do not dig there now."

title: An Armourer's Notes on the Dread Totem
text:
"Notes of Gunnar Lodd, armourer, made while taking apart on my bench a Dread Totem from the western clearing.
The totems are built the way the mound-folk built their coats. Split bone, antler tines mostly, laid like fish scales, each overlapping the one below it by a third, laced through two holes with gut boiled in salt. A blade that strikes it slides along the scales instead of biting.
I copied the lacing for my own coat, over a layer of boiled leather. Two men struck at it with a falchion for an hour, and not one scale cracked.
The rest I did not copy. At the heart of every totem there is a skull with its jaw wired shut, and it is the skull that sends out the fear, every twelve breaths, steady as a bell. I put mine in a sack and dropped it in the river."

title: The Song in the Silk
text:
"Taken down by Corporal Wim Doran from what the thing in the silk sang during the night watches at the south mound, as near as I could follow it.
'He said the god would take me for a bride and the rain would come. I wore the grey pearls. I lay down on the stone in my wedding linen and I was not afraid. The god came out of the trees and looked at me with his green eyes, and his antlers dripped on my face, and then he turned and walked away. He did not want me. The rain came all the same.
Then the small ones came up from under the stone to keep me warm. They are gentle. They are always hungry. I let them.
Ruprecht, I hear your boots at the edge of the clearing every night. Come in. I have kept your side of the bed.'
By the third night it was using my name. I have asked to be moved to the north watch."

title: The Final Hunt
text:
"Statement of Gerrit Vos, huntsman to the late margrave, given at Haske Hall.
In the third dry summer my lord rode out to hunt the god the old priests called Cernunnos. He took sixteen riders, the best of the kennel and the great horn. He said that a god who would not take what he was given could be made to give.
We found its tracks at the eastern ring: hoofprints the size of a shield, and every dolmen along the way broken across the middle, as if something had run through them head down. The hounds would not follow. They lay flat and wet themselves, every one.
My lord went on alone. I heard him blow the great horn once, deep in the trees, and a long while later twice more, which in our calls means the quarry has turned and the riders are to follow. We did not follow.
We have heard the horn every night since, a little closer each time. I would know that horn anywhere. It is my lord's horn. I no longer believe that it is my lord blowing it."

title: Genesis of the Hollow Sovereign
text:
"From the chronicle of the abbey at Mardale, in the year the river froze. The king we now call the Hollow Sovereign ordered a stair cut into the hill beneath his tower, to find what his surveyors had heard knocking under the foundations. The masons were paid by the step. They were paid well the first year and very well after that.
At the fortieth flight they broke into a burial vault that no one had dug. Below it they found drains, and below the drains a hall of cold furnaces. Each level was older than the one above it and built by other hands, and none of the hands were ours. The masons stopped asking to be paid by the step. They asked to be paid by the day, and then to be let go.
In the ninth year the king went down himself with his household, and on his order the stair was walled up behind him. In spring the wall was opened to send down bread. The carriers came back after eleven days. They had found neither the household nor the end of the stair, and they swore that the first forty flights had become fifty."

title: The Quartermaster's Accounts
text:
"Accounts kept by Joss Dask, quartermaster to the Brisk company, for the descent. Floors one to nine: Archibald the Gilded on seven, the demon Malphas on two. Never both on one floor. Never neither.
Archibald's coin: thick, good gold, no king's head and no mint mark. He weighs ours and gives a fair rate. He has never once asked where we came in.
Malphas takes no coin. For his door he took some of the strength from Margit's arms, and he sold her a pact potion that she says tastes of her own blood. He was polite. He asked after Archibald by name, the way you ask after a neighbour you are suing.
Floor ten: Archibald. I paid him with coins we took off a dead man in the Foundry. He bit one, looked at me for a long moment, and said he had wondered where that one had got to. Then he gave me my change in the same coin."

title: The Locksmith's Report
text:
"Report of Master Cyprian Holm, locksmith, on the key brought to him by the Brisk company. Gold over a core I cannot identify without cutting it, which I was not permitted to do. Warm in the hand, warmer than the hand. No maker's mark. The bit is cut for a lock of five wards, and no two keys I have been shown have the same wards.
The company says such keys turn up once a floor if at all: in the grip of some champion among the monsters, in a chest, or on the thing at the bottom. Each opens Archibald's vault on its own floor and no other. A key carried down the stair unused is lead by the next landing.
I have the lead one here. It is lead through and through, it has the same five wards, and I would swear to that in any court. I asked who cuts them. The company did not know. I asked what a champion of the dead wants with the key to a moneylender's door, and they had no answer to that either."

title: The Five Seals of the Chasm
text:
"The pilgrims who went down before the companies kept one rule at every threshold. Where the stone changes, stop. Stand on the last step of the old floor and breathe the air of the new one until your body stops fighting it: the damp of the Crypt, the reek of the Sewers, the heat of the Foundry, the dust of the Archives, the cold of the Kurgan.
The guides said each of the five is shut with its own seal, and that the body must be let in through each one slowly, the way a hand is let into cold water. Guides who skipped the stop did not last. Those who kept it came back up with more blood and breath in them than they took down.
After the fifth threshold the stone changes again. No pilgrim wrote down what it changed into, or how many times."

title: The Ownerless Book
effect_text: +1 Skill Point & +5 Stat Points (Permanent Free Allocation)
text:
"This book has no author. Each owner writes on the first blank leaf, the writing is gone by morning, and the owner is a little different. A copyist of the Archives wrote 'steadier hands' and copied for fifty years without a blot. A sergeant of the wardens wrote that he wished to be harder to kill, and he was.
The rules are on the inside of the cover, in many hands, each owner adding one. Write about yourself and no one else. Write a little. Do not write your name. Pass the book on before you need it again.
The last rule is scratched in so hard that it went through to the board: do not ask it who built the dungeon. Under it, in fresh ink, someone has written the first half of an answer and stopped."

title: Work Order for the Lower Doors
text:
"Work order, the abbey forge. To Master Odran, smith, from the prior's office.
Replace the iron door, gallery four, east. Replace the iron door, gallery four, west. Replace the iron door, gallery six, the bone store. Replace the iron door, gallery seven. Replace the iron door, gallery seven, again.
Odran's reply, on the back: I will forge them, but I want it written down that none of the old doors was broken. The hinge pins were lifted out, the way you lift a door off to oil it, and the doors are gone, and each one weighs as much as two men. Your Watch tells me they have seen one since, in the north vaults, carried in front of something that walks behind it."

title: Letter from the Pendulum Wright
text:
"Teodor Haas, wright, to the Prior of Saint Ilse.
Reverend Prior, I write again about the eleven crowns still owed to my family for the scythes in the narrow corridors of the king's vaults. My grandfather hung them on the order of King Morvath's steward: six blades of black iron on oak arms, swung by counterweights, each passing once in the time it takes a man to walk four steps. The steward said they were to keep thieves out. My grandfather noted in his book that the blades were hung with their edges toward the inner end of each corridor, toward the hall, not toward the stair.
In the spring I went down to see whether they could be sold back for the iron. They are running. Sixty years since anyone wound them, yet the counterweights are up and the pivots are greased with fresh tallow. I did not stay to find out who greases them. I would like my eleven crowns."

title: Rules of Tam Hollis's Crew
text:
"Rules of Tam Hollis's crew for going under the abbey. Learn them before your first descent; nobody will say them twice.
One. The plates are the flagstones with a finger-wide gap all round and no dust in the gap. Two. The spikes come up hip-high and go back down; the man on the plate gets them, and so does the man beside him. Three. The footmen never step on the plates. Watch where the bones walk, and walk there.
Four. If a skeleton is standing on a plate, somebody put it there. Leave that corridor. Five. Nobody counts the take until we are up the stair."

title: On the Unlit Passages
text:
"Master, you asked me to record the effect in the crypt corridors. Here it is, as plainly as I can put it. In the lit vaults my strength comes back to me at the usual rate, a little slower than at home on account of the damp. In the unlit passages it comes back at half that, near enough; I timed it twice against the sandglass. The sergeant who went with me says it is the same with him, that his anger 'goes slack' in the dark and he has to keep hold of it like a dog on a lead.
I do not think the darkness itself is the cause. The cold under the abbey takes warmth from whatever it can, and in a lit room the torch gives it something else to drink. I would not stake my name on that. This much I can say for certain: carry two torches, and do not let the warriors carry them, because they drop them the moment anything comes at them."

title: Catechism of the Choir
text:
"Catechism of the Choir, for those who would take the grey. The first sheet; the second was not found.
What is the Choir? Those who sing the dead back into service. Why do we sing? Because the king promised that none of his would rot alone, and somebody must keep a promise.
How many breaths? Eight. On the eighth the bones remember their shape. How near must the singer stand? Near enough to hear them settle; thirty feet at most, for past that the bones do not listen. And if the bones are crushed? Then they are dust, and dust does not remember. Keep the living away from them, the ones with hammers above all.
What shall we be given? Places in the hall, at the king's right hand, in the first rank. Who has seen the hall? No one who sings has come back from it yet."

title: The Arrowsmith's Report on Bone Heads
text:
"Gisela Rook, arrowsmith to the Crypt Watch, on the arrows taken out of wounded men.
Of the arrows drawn from our men this month I have kept twenty-two. The shafts are ordinary ash, and old; some come from our own armoury, the one we lost in the west gallery. The heads are not iron. They are bone, splinters of shin and rib ground to a needle on stone and bound on with gut. They go through mail where an iron head would catch, because the rings spread and the bone slips between them.
Once in, they break. Half the splinter stays in the wound, and the men limp and drag the leg for an hour afterwards, even from a shallow hit. The surgeon has stopped trying to dig them all out.
Somebody down there makes these, and with care."

title: From the Inquest into a Mason's Death
text:
"From the inquest into the death of Ruprecht Kale, mason. Witness: his partner, Wil Dorr.
Q. Where were you working? A. Relaying the floor in the north vault, gallery five. The flags kept coming up. Q. Coming up how? A. From underneath. We thought it was the frost. Then one came up under Ruprecht while he was kneeling on it.
Q. Describe what came up. A. Legs. A great many legs, and a mouth like a leech. It bit him on the calf and went back under before I had the hammer up. Q. Did he die of the bite? A. No. After it he couldn't lift his hands, couldn't close them on the trowel. It took him a long time to get his hammer to his shoulder, and it bit him again while he was trying.
Q. Why did you not help him? A. It got me first, on the wrist. Look at it. I still can't write my name, so you'll have to put it down for me."

title: Infirmary Ledger of Saint Ilse
text:
"Infirmary ledger of the convent of Saint Ilse, kept by Sister Gerlind, winter of the second year.
Day 3. Wat Harle, carter, the fever. Sprinkled by the Prioress at vespers. By morning sitting up and taking broth. Day 5. Wat Harle will not eat bread. He took a hen from the kitchen yard and ate it raw in the latrine, and afterwards he wept. Says he is ashamed and hungry at the same time.
Day 6. Elsbet Moor, the fever, sprinkled. Up by noon. The same hunger by evening.
Day 9. Wat Harle tied to his bed after biting Sister Brigid on the hand. The Prioress ordered the bite washed with font water. I washed it with well water and said nothing.
Day 11. Sister Brigid has stopped eating bread."

title: Contract for a Keening Woman
text:
"Contract between the parish of Coldharrow and Mag Tully, keening woman, for the vigil over the Harrow family, in the second year of the Long Winter.
The said Mag Tully shall keen in the Harrow vault from dusk to dawn for nine nights, never falling silent for longer than one paternoster, so that the dead do not think themselves forgotten. Wage: sixpence a night, bread, small beer and one candle.
Should the said Mag Tully take the fever during the vigil, she shall not leave the vault, lest she carry it up. Should she die, she shall be laid with the family she keened for, by way of recompense, and the wage for the remaining nights shall be paid to her sister.
Her mark: a cross. Pinned below is the sister's receipt for four nights' wage."

title: The King's Burial Accounts
text:
"From the household accounts of King Morvath: the costs of the burial, kept by Hal Wymark, steward.
For ermine to line the burial robe, sixty skins: four crowns. For the mace of black iron, cast by the founders under the burning hill to His Majesty's own measure in the summer before his death, and tried by him in the yard: eleven crowns. For three hundred plain swords for the soldiers' shelves, which His Majesty ordered were not to be blunted: thirty crowns. To the bearers who moved the coffin of the princess Aude from the abbey to lie at the king's feet: one crown.
In the steward's hand: His Majesty asked that the shelves be cut wider than custom, so that a man might sit up on them, and I have paid the masons for it. At his order I have also left the great hall without a door."

title: A Letter from Bishop Marrach
text:
"Reverend Mother Vespera, your report of eleven sick raised from their beds in a single week was read aloud in chapter and has been sent on to the Primate. I need not tell you what it means for this see that our convent should be the house the Lord has chosen, in a winter when every other house in the province is burying its own sisters.
I must ask for more. The Primate's legate arrives at Candlemas and will want to see a sick man rise with his own eyes. Choose one whose family is known in the town. Do not trouble me with what your infirmarian writes about their diet; the sick are always strange about their food.
I am sending you a new aspergillum of silver, with a longer handle, since you wrote that your hands are tired."

title: A Soldier's Letter Home
text:
"Anna, we are two levels down now and the pay has come through, so you can stop asking the baker for credit. There are two things you should know, and better you hear them from me.
On every level there is a room where two doors stand side by side. The gilt one belongs to a merchant called Archibald, who opens only to whoever brings the key, and nobody on our level found the key. The other door is red, and the one behind it does not want money. He took his price from me before I was over the threshold. It does not hurt. I am only weaker in the arm than I was, and I will stay that way. After that the door stood open for the others, so they did not have to pay.
What I bought with it is a flask the sergeant says will keep me alive in the king's hall. I am not to drink it before then. I will write after. Piet."

title: A Page from Archibald's Daybook
text:
"A page from the daybook of Archibald the Gilded, in his own hand. The crypt level.
Bought: one longsword, White Hawk pattern, notched, from a lady with no right hand; eight gold. Bought: a bundle of grey robes, bloodied, from a party of four who would not say where they got them; three gold, washing at my expense.
Sold: nineteen torches at four gold the torch, the price having doubled since the wailing began in the north vaults. Sold: one healing draught to the same lady, on credit, which I do not give, and which I note here so that I remember why I did.
Note: the key for this level was brought in by a boy who had taken it from a dead wight's belt. He asked me who makes the keys. I told him that was not a question for a man without coin."

title: What the Wight Teaches
text:
"Sergeant Brannoch the younger, son of the armourer, to the new intake.
You will meet a wight carrying a door, and you will hit the door, and nothing will happen. Before you curse it, watch how it holds the thing. It does not stand square. It turns the door a hand's breadth off true, so your blow skids along the iron instead of landing, and it leans its whole weight in behind, shoulder to the boards.
Do the same with your own plate. A breastplate that takes a blow square will dent and crack the ribs behind it. Taken at a slant, with your weight forward and your chin down, the blow runs off along the steel. My father makes good armour, but it is only as good as the angle you give it."

title: The Rule of Saint Ilse: On Night Vigils
text:
"From the Rule of Saint Ilse, the chapter on vigils, as the sisters kept it before the Long Winter.
A sister who watches over the dead in the lower chapels shall eat before she goes down, not after: bread, a cup of broth and salt on the tongue. She shall wear wool next to the skin and linen over it, never the reverse.
She shall not kneel on the bare stone, which drinks the heat from the knees until the legs fail, but on a folded cloak. Every hour she shall rise, walk the length of the chapel and back, and breathe slowly through the nose, four counts in and four counts out.
A sister who keeps this rule may sit a vigil from compline to lauds for nine nights and climb the stair unaided. Those who thought themselves above it had to be carried up."

title: The Red Second
text:
"Men who have served below a long time learn something I have never seen taught above ground. When they strike, they take something back. You can see it: a man cut across the arm at the start of a fight is standing straight by the end of it, and he has not stopped to bind the wound.
I asked old Dane how it is done. He said it lies in the second after the blade bites, the red second, when the other man flinches. You do not pull back in that second. You lean in, breathe with his flinch, and let it come up your arm. He said he learned it from watching the ghouls feed and is not proud of it.
I have entered it in the officers' book all the same, and I have told the chaplain nothing."

title: Scout's Report from the Chapter Crypt
text:
"Report of Corporal Nell Ashby, scout, to Captain Hesk.
The chapter crypt under the convent is hers now. I watched through the grating for as long as two candles take to burn down.
She does not walk. She hangs a little above the floor, and her feet do not touch it. Her hands are the silver aspergillum from the bishop, or they have grown into it; I could not tell which. When she lifts them, flies come out of the walls, enough to put out a lantern, and when she sings, everyone in the room hurts behind the eyes. Once she pressed her thumb to the brow of one of the shambling sisters, and a little later that sister burst apart and took the two standing beside her with her. Near the end she opened something on her back that I first took for her cloak, and rose up into the vault.
There are two shrines in that crypt, by the east and west walls, still consecrated as far as I know. When the flies passed the west one, they went round it.
I recommend that we go in no fewer than four, and that somebody carries oil and flint for both shrines."

title: Left at the Crypt Gate
text:
"Kept by the porter of Saint Ilse: things left by the townsfolk at the upper crypt gate in the year after it was sealed.
A wreath of rue. A child's shoe, the left one. Bread every Sunday from the Moor house. A letter addressed to 'Wat', unopened; I have kept it. A whetstone. Three candles, lit. A White Hawk badge with the pin bent flat. Bread from the Moor house.
From midsummer the bread is gone every Monday morning, and the candles are burning again when I come by at dawn, though I hold the only key to the outer gate.
Last entry: a lantern standing on the inside of the bars, lit, and next to it the whetstone, worn hollow in the middle."

title: On the Drain beneath the Abbey
text:
"Master Joss Calloway, engineer to the lower town, to the cellarer of the abbey.
Sir, you asked where the abbey cistern drains when it overflows. I have traced it for you at the town's expense, which I will ask you to repay. It runs out under the north wall of the crypt through a culvert of the old kingdom and falls into our main sewer under the tanners' quarter, a mile downhill.
Hence my letter. Since the convent began drawing on the cistern in earnest, my men below the tanners' quarter have been going down with a fever that will not break, and two of them have left their posts and not come up again. The sewer chapel down there, which the town closed years ago, has candles burning in it.
I ask that the culvert be bricked up at your end. If you will not do it, I will brick it up at mine, and then your crypt will flood instead of my sewers."

title: Interrogation of a Choir Novice
text:
"Interrogation of a novice of the Choir, name withheld, taken in the west gallery. Present: Captain Hesk and Saltash, clerk.
Q. Have you seen the king? A. Once, from the stair. He sits. Sitting, he is taller than you are standing.
Q. What is in the hall? A. His men, on the shelves. And lids hung from the roof on chains, the old lids from the sarcophagi; we hung them ourselves, a few every year. Q. For what purpose? A. He said they were his rain.
Q. What becomes of the bones you raise and lose? A. They go to him. When the hall is short of men, he takes in the broken ones and wears them. The living he keeps in a cage of bone spears until he has a hand free.
Q. Why did you leave the Choir? A. I did not leave. I was sent up to count you."

title: Inquisitor Pesk's First Report
text:
"To His Grace the Bishop of Dunmark, from Halvard Pesk, Inquisitor. I went below on the feast of Saint Odo with twelve men of the Cathedral guard and a ratcatcher to guide us. We came back with nine men and without the ratcatcher, who had been paid in advance.
The Low Church is larger than the Chapter believes. In the dye-works sump we found an altar of stacked grates and before it fresh candles, bought in the city: the chandler's mark was on them. Someone above is supplying them. We found a surgeon's table with straps, and on it a ratman larger than a man, asleep, with fresh stitches. We killed it in its sleep, and it took four of us.
I request forty men, lamp oil, and authority to question the chandlers' guild. I do not request more ratcatchers. They know too much about the drains and too little about loyalty."

title: The Lamplighter's Tally
text:
"Lamps of the Long Gallery, lit at the evening bell by Widow Hanne Kettle, lamplighter. Lamps one to twenty-four, all lit. Oil used: two quarts.
The same. At the third hour the mist came up from the canal and put out lamps twenty-four, twenty-three and twenty-two, in that order, slowly, one every hundred steps. I relit them.
The same, every night this week. Always from the far end and in order, at the pace of someone walking. Last night it stopped at lamp eleven, which hangs beside my stool. The mist stood there a long while. Then lamp eleven went out, and the mist went back the way it came. I have applied for the post at the Cathedral. They have stairs there, and windows."

title: The Runner's Rule
text:
"The Water Office pays a runner a penny a message to carry orders between the pump houses, and the route runs past the acid spouts on Alchemists' Row, under the Lobbers' ledges and over the drowned steps. I have run it for six years. This is how.
Never watch what is thrown. Watch the thrower. A Sludge Lobber rocks back on its heels before it heaves, and if you move then, you are clear before the mud leaves its hands. A spout hisses for one breath before it fires. Count, but listen as well, because rust does not always keep time.
And never jump wide; a wide jump lands you in the next trap. Step small and to the side, with your weight on the back foot, so that you can step again at once. They pay me a penny. I have never once been burned."

title: Letter Left in a Lever Housing
text:
"Ned. The Water Office has you listed as lost below Gate Seven with Hob Tanner, and they have stopped your wage from the day you went down. I do not believe them. Hob's wife says she heard Hob in the cellar drain three nights running, saying her name.
I paid a flusher two shillings to put this where you would put your hand, in the housing of the lever at Gate Seven. If you read it, come up by the dye-works steps. Do not come by the cellar drain. The children are frightened of it, and so am I.
If you cannot come up, leave something in the housing so that I know. Your knife, or the ring. Anything. I will send the man down again on Saint Gerlind's day.
Below, in charcoal, in another hand: 'Went back on the saint's day. Letter still here, unopened. Ring on top of it.'"

title: Prices at the Gutter Market
text:
"Prices at the market under the Weir Quarter bridge, copied in autumn by an informer of the Cathedral.
Rat tails, by the dozen: one farthing. A hand for stitching on, fresh, the fingers still working: four shillings. Grey serum from the Stitchers, by the thimble: one crown, or a cup of your own blood. Lamp oil: dearer than above. Dry boots: dearest of all; nobody would name a price.
A woman sells keys on a string, iron and brass, guaranteed to open any floodgate housing from Gate One to Gate Eight. Asked for a key to Gate Nine, she laughed. Asked whether anyone sells gold keys, she said the gentleman who wants those does not come to markets; he waits in his own room for them to be brought to him, and he pays fairly, which is how you know he is not from here."

title: The Tanner's Boy Testifies
text:
"Testimony of Abel, apprentice to Master Dorn, tanner, about eleven years old, taken by the ward constable.
He says he was sent at dusk to rinse hides at the Sluice steps with Will Garrow, a journeyman. The water was brown and flat. Will knelt on the bottom step. The boy saw the water rise behind Will in a long shape, without a sound, like a wet hide being lifted, and it had arms. It struck Will once at the back of the neck and then threw a handful of mud into the boy's face.
When he had cleared his eyes, Will was lying face down on the step and the water was flat again. Asked why he did not run for help, he said he could no longer tell where the water ended. The boy has since refused to wash."

title: Petition of a Mole-Rat Keeper
text:
"To the Ward Court of the Weir Quarter. The petition of Osk Fennick, keeper of blind mole-rats for the glove-makers' trade, whose beasts give the softest hide in Dunmark.
On the night after Candlemas my best breeding animal, a white female the size of a pony, was taken from her pen. The pen was dug under, not broken. The tunnel led down to the drains. The constable followed it as far as Gate Six and would go no further.
A flusher has since told me that a white mole-rat of that size is ridden in the lower drains by a ratman in robes who carries a smoking pot. Sirs, she was gentle and blind and would follow any hand that fed her. I ask the court for her value, which is eleven crowns, and that whoever meets her should not hurt her, for she does not know what she carries."

title: The Coroner's Memorandum on the Drowned
text:
"To the Water Office, from the City Coroner, regarding the bodies in the drains.
The drains are used to dispose of the dead whom no one will pay to bury: paupers, foundlings, the hanged, and those found in the Weir Quarter with a knife between their ribs. In open water a body bloats and rises in three days. In the drains it cannot rise, because the vaults hold it down, and the gas gathers under the brick in pockets. Bring a lamp near one and it goes off.
I must also report that the bodies do not stay where they are put. Of twelve I marked with lead tags in the overflow at Gate Four, I have recovered three. The canal watch tells me the rest came back up the channels against the current and burst when the men came near. I recommend that the dead of the city be burned. The Cathedral has refused, holding that the dead must be whole for the resurrection."

title: Sister Imma's Rule for the Tainted
text:
"From the day book of the Hospice of Saint Ambrel at the Sluice steps, kept by Sister Imma for the sisters who come after.
Men come up from the sludge with the taint in them. Their wounds will not close, and every bandage does less than the last. Do not waste prayers on it; the taint does not listen. Take them to the dry flags of the cloister and make them stand, not sit, on stone that has not seen water, until it leaves them.
Then the broth: bones, barley and a handful of nettles, boiled until the spoon stands. Then sleep. The next morning, the same. A man who keeps this rule for a season comes up from the drains each time with more life in him than he took down. I have kept it thirty years in this damp house and have not once been ill."

title: Edict Against the Low Church
text:
"By authority of the Chapter of Saint Odo, the following doctrines, preached in the lower parishes of Dunmark and beneath them, are declared heresy, and those who hold them are cut off from the sacraments:
That what is thrown away is not lost but offered. That the dead belong to the water and not to the earth. That the rats of the city are a congregation and may be preached to. That the saints were buried above the drains so that the drains might feed on them. That rain is a sacrament.
Let every chapel of the Weir Quarter be shut and its bell taken down. Let no one sell candles, oil or bread at the grates. Given at Dunmark under seal. Added by the Chapter clerk the following year: the chapels were shut and the sales forbidden; the congregation has since doubled; the candles still arrive."

title: Questioning of a Ratman
text:
"Record of questioning, Cathedral cellars. The prisoner is a ratman taken alive at Gate Six after it threw a flask of filth and blinded two of the guard. Present: Inquisitor Pesk, the clerk, and Jory Hesketh, ratcatcher, who claims to understand its speech.
Asked its name, it made a sound Hesketh gives as 'Seventh of the litter'. Asked who leads it: 'The one who rides.' Asked where he rides: 'Down. Always down, under the bell.' Asked what the bell is for: 'For you. So you see your friends as they are.'
Asked why the Low Church shelters it, it showed its teeth, which Hesketh says is laughter, and said: 'Who shelters who?' The prisoner died in the night of no wound we could find. Hesketh has been dismissed for refusing to translate further. He said that what it was telling him was not meant for the clerk."

title: Payroll of the Lower Gangs
text:
"Water Office payroll, lower gangs, week of the spring flood.
Ulm, foreman: twelve shillings. Mullen: eight. Tanner, Hob: eight, stopped from Tuesday, lost below Gate Seven. Harl, Ned: eight, stopped from Tuesday, lost below Gate Seven. Pell, runner: fourteen messages at a penny. Widow Kettle, lamps: four shillings, less sixpence for spilled oil.
Deducted from the gang, by custom: one shilling a man toward hooks and lost lamps. Paid to the wives of the lost: nothing, the bodies not being recovered. Note by the clerk: Harl's wife came to the window for his wage and said she had heard from him. I told her a man listed as lost cannot be paid. She said he had not asked for money."

title: The Stitcher's Apprentice Writes Home
text:
"Mother, I am well, and do not believe what Aunt Grete tells you. I am not a beggar in the drains. I am apprenticed to a surgeon, a real one, who studied at the College before they quarrelled with him, and I eat every day.
The work is hard. We mend the brothers who are hurt fighting the Cathedral men, and we make them stronger than they were. Master says the body is a draft, not a fair copy, and that God left it unfinished on purpose so that we would have something to do. I hold the lamp and the needle, and I am learning the knots.
Yesterday Master showed me where my own arm could be improved, at the elbow, with a second joint, and asked if I would like it. I said I would think about it. He said there was no hurry. Please send the grey wool stockings. It is very damp here."

title: Catwalk Drill of the Canal Watch
text:
"Drill for recruits of the Canal Watch, to be learned before any man is sent over the canals below Gate Five, where the only path is the old iron catwalk, a foot wide and without a rail.
First week: walk the chalk line in the yard with a full bucket in each hand. Spill, and you walk it again. Second week: the same at a run, while the sergeant throws wet rags at you. Third week: the beam over the dye vat, blindfolded, turning at the end without stopping.
Keep the knees soft. Look at the far end of the walk, never at your feet and never at the water, because sometimes the water looks back. A man who has done the drill fights on a catwalk as easily as on the parade ground, and turns faster on any ground than a man who has not."

title: What the Lobbers Throw
text:
"Report of Sergeant Molk, Canal Watch, on the mud thrown by the creatures called Lobbers, at the request of the Water Office, which wishes to know whether it can be cleared with shovels.
It cannot. We collected a bucket of it after the fight at the dye-works steps. It is heavier than river mud and does not settle. When a man steps in it, it takes hold of the boot and pulls, not hard but steadily, and lets go only after it has held a while, as if it were counting. In the bucket it did the same to a stick.
When we washed it we found it full of hair, human, much of it long and some of it braided, and a few small horn buttons. The Lobbers scoop it from the pool below Drain Head where the big thing lies. I advise the Water Office not to ask what the big thing is made of. I have had the bucket taken back down."

title: A Bargain at the Red Door
text:
"Deacon Ibbot of the Low Church, to the brothers who go deeper after me.
Below Gate Nine there is a room with a door of dry red stone, and nothing else in our drains is dry. The one inside calls himself a broker. He did not ask for coin. When I crossed the threshold something went out of me, and since then I cannot close my right hand on my staff. He said it was the toll, and a very small one.
He offered me a contract: my sight in the dark for my sleep. I signed. I see in the black water now as well as by day, and I have not slept in forty-one days. I write to tell you to read the contract twice. He wants you to read it once. He enjoyed it very much when I did."

title: Inventory of the Grating at Tanner's Sluice
text:
"Items taken from the great grating at Tanner's Sluice at the spring clearing, as recorded for the Water Office. Anything of value is handed to the Ward.
Boots, odd, forty-two. Boots, pairs, three. A child's wooden horse. Rings, iron and copper, eleven; one of silver, engraved 'G.R.', handed to the Ward. A Cathedral candlestick, bent. A bell clapper, bronze, very large, without its bell. Hair, braided, a quantity. A Canal Watch cap with the badge cut off. A pot of salve from the sign of the Ladle, still sealed.
Also a lead tag of the Coroner's office, numbered seven, wired to nothing. Also three Dunmark pennies of this year's mint, laid in a row on the crossbar of the grating, which the gang swear were not there when they began work."

title: Minutes of the Council on Gate Nine
text:
"Minutes of the Water Office Council, third sitting after the spring flood. Present: the Master of Conduits, four aldermen, the clerk. Alderman Ruel absent, still not found.
Moved: that Gate Nine be shut, chained, and its lever taken out, on the advice of the former engineer Grell, now in Saltgate prison. Objected: that Gate Nine carries a quarter of the Weir Quarter's waste, and without it the cellars will flood. Answered by the Master of Conduits: the cellars flood now, from below, with water that is warm.
Carried, four to one. The lever is to be taken out and melted down. Added the following month: the lever was removed and the chains set. At the next inspection the gate was found open, the chains whole and still locked, the lever back in its housing, and a fresh mark in the rust where a hand had gripped it."

title: Words Scratched Above a Dry Ledge
text:
"Scratched into the brick over the dry ledge at the bend below Gate Eight, in several hands. Copied by Sergeant Molk of the Canal Watch, who asks that someone come and tell him what the last line means.
'Saint Ambrel keep the water low.' Under it: 'He did not.' Under that, deeper, with a knife: 'Seven of us on the ledge. The gate shut behind us. The lever on the left is rusted to the wall, do not waste your strength on it, pull the right one twice.' Then seven names. Six are crossed out, each in a different hand. The seventh is not.
Below the names, low down by the waterline, small, scratched with something that was not a knife: 'Thank you for the gift.'"

title: Inquisitor Pesk's Last Report
text:
"To His Grace the Bishop, from Halvard Pesk. This will be my last report, and I ask that it be read aloud in Chapter and not only filed.
We have burned the Low Church out of the dye-works, the market and the chapels of the Weir Quarter. It has made no difference. Each time we clear a level, the congregation turns up one level lower, and larger. Your Grace, they are not hiding from us. They go down because something calls them down, and our raids only hurry them along.
I have stood at the rail over the great sump at Drain Head and watched the thing in it breathe. I saw the candles we confiscated floating lit on its back. I have heard the bell. On the feast of Saint Odo I take the remaining men below Gate Nine. If I do not write again, send no other inquisitor. Seal the grates. And stop buying the chandler's candles yourself, Your Grace. I have the receipts."

title: Work Order 3118
text:
"Work Order 3118. From the Purser of the Prince to the Galt Works. For the new west hall: forty grates, cast iron, four feet square, each hung on four pins. Price agreed: nine groats the grate.
Margin, in the Works clerk's hand: nine groats will not cover wrought pins. Proposed: pins cast of the common grey metal, at a third of the cost. Grey metal softens under heat from below, and the hall stands over the melt. Margin, in the Purser's hand: the hall is for barrows, not for standing. Proceed.
Margin, clerk: proceeded. Forty grates hung on the fourth of the month. Grate eleven fell on the twelfth with a barrowman on it, Lodo Hanf, aged nineteen. Grate eleven rehung, grey pins.
Margin, Purser: noted. The Prince asks that the west hall be finished by the feast without further cost."

title: Liesl's Letter to Her Mother
text:
"Mother, you asked why Jost does not write. He is well, as far as I know, and fed better than I am. He has gone over to the Pact.
They came to the barracks on rest day with white bread and a jug, and they did not preach, which is how they get the young ones. They asked which of us had been burned. Jost held up his hand with the two bars on it. The man in the red apron showed him his own arms, burned to the elbow and healed smooth and shining like glazed pots, and said the fire had taken all it wanted from him and would never take more. That was all. Jost went with them that night.
I have seen him once since, across the casting floor. He was walking barefoot through the spill from the cauldrons. He smiled at me. There was a mark drawn on his chest in something that glowed when he breathed, and the men around him kept their distance from it, and he did not seem to mind.
Pray for him, but do not light a candle. I do not think he would want one now."

title: Regulations of the Galt Works
text:
"Regulations of the Galt Works, posted at the lower gate by order of the Forgemaster. Ignorance of them is no defence and no ground for compensation.
I. No man is to wear his own armour on the lower floors. The heat works the rivets loose and the straps dry and stretch, and a man who fights in it for long ends the fight in worse armour than he began it. Works aprons are issued at cost. II. The wall vents cough before they fire. When a vent coughs, the man in front of it moves. The Works is not answerable for men who finished their sentence first.
III. The cauldrons of the long hall boil over on a count of six. Learn the count of your cauldron. IV. The lower gate is closed from the last bell to the first. Persons wishing to leave the Works during these hours are to apply to the taskmaster on duty, who will not let them."

title: Confession of a Taskmaster
text:
"Written for Father Lorenz, because I cannot say it to his face.
The hook is a simple tool. You throw it, it bites, you pull, the man comes to you, and before he finds his feet you set the brand. It all happens in one breath, and you do not look at the face, because you are looking at the hand you are going to mark. I have done it more times than I have eaten hot meals.
On the eleventh I threw at a man running for the flue on the west gantry. He was quick and I was quicker. When he came in under me he said my name, my house name that nobody here knows, and the brand was on him before I understood. It was Emil. I had not seen him in nine years. I did not know he had been sold to the Works.
He has two bars and a cross now. The cross is mine. There is no mark for a third attempt, Father, you know what that means, and he will try again, because he is my brother and that is the kind we are. I am asking you what I should do when I see him run."

title: Archibald's Foundry Ledger
text:
"Ledger of Archibald the Gilded, Foundry chamber, the week the Key came late. Bought: one breastplate, good steel, the straps shrunk to string by the heat, the rivets loose in their holes. Paid four silver and told the seller it was generous, which it was. Heat does not ruin steel. It ruins the man inside it, who forgets to tighten anything until it is too late, and then sells to me.
Bought: one taskmaster's hook, still warm. Paid nothing; the seller did not want it in his pack. Sold: six torches, two healing draughts, one mace at a markup I am not ashamed of. A party that has met a carapace will pay anything for a mace.
Not sold: a soldered tin from the cauldron hall. The seller swore it held soul-iron and wanted thirty gold. I sent him across the corridor. My colleague across the corridor deals in that kind of goods, and in that kind of customer. I heard his door. I did not hear the man come out."

title: Terms of the Ichor
text:
"Terms offered by Malphas in his chamber on the Foundry floor, copied out by the undersigned for his own records before he signed.
The party of the first part surrenders, for the rest of his descent, a measure of his hardness: that part of a man which turns a blow aside. He keeps his armour. It will simply serve him worse. In return he receives one flask of Hellfire Ichor, which burns cold going down and for the space of a minute makes him faster than anything in these halls, hounds and revenants included.
The broker adds, in his own hand and unasked: 'I have made this exchange on this floor before, with a smith who wanted more hands. He remains my best customer. Ask him how he likes his skin.'
Signed below: Bertil Kayne, sergeant. Under the name, later, in pencil, a tally of six strokes, one for each fight since, and beside the last: straps gone at the shoulder, two ribs."

title: On Finding Cold Shuts
text:
"Wiebke Loew, chief inspector of castings, for whoever takes her bench. Every casting has a fault. Metal poured from two sides meets in the middle, and if it has cooled a hair too much on the way it never truly joins. We call it a cold shut: a fine line, often filled with scale, and you would swear the piece was whole. Strike it once on that line and it falls in two.
You find it by learning how the metal flowed: where the pour began, where the streams went, where they had to meet. Look there. After a year you see the shut before the casting.
I can no longer look at anything else. When a man in harness walks toward me, I find myself asking where his pieces meet: the buckle, the gorget, the gap under the arm."

title: Losses of the Seventh Shift
text:
"Losses of the seventh shift, month of Ashfall, for the paymaster, so that no wage is paid to the dead.
Hob Tarry, barrowman: grate, west hall. Ilse Durn, cauldron crew: splash, cauldron four, on the count she had been getting wrong for a year without harm. Matthis Brenner and Udo Krall, gantry: hound, the new litter, armour gone in the first breath and the rest of them after. Yann, no second name, flue boy: imp, burned on the ladder, fell. Old Bernat, striker: struck in the casting hall by a Punisher that ran on his own rhythm and did not stop when he stepped in front of it to fix a pin.
Paymaster's note: Hob Tarry also appears among the losses of the third shift, month of Embers, grate, west hall. Same man, same marks on the hand. Find out whether he was paid in between, and by whom, and for whom."

title: The Revenant on the Third Gantry
text:
"Watch log, third gantry, kept by Rudi Vogt, night watch. First night: a light on the gantry at the fourth bell, man-high, walking the rail from the crane to the pour gate and back. It went through the tool shed without using the door. The boards burned along its path behind it, and for a short while nobody could cross. I did not report it.
Third night: the same route, the same bell. I timed it. It stops at the pour gate for as long as it takes to open a sluice and then turns back. That was Gunther's job. Gunther went into the trench in the spring.
Fifth night: the new sluiceman did not know to step aside. It did not go round him. Nothing of him burned, they tell me, except the inside. I have reported it now. The taskmasters say the watch is to keep to the north side of the gantry from the fourth bell, and that the sluice must still be opened at the fourth bell. The sluice duty is to be drawn by lot."

title: Mina Haller's Copybook
text:
"Copybook of Mina Haller, aged eight. Lines set on rest day by the master from the Pact.
Set: The Mother sleeps under the Works and keeps us warm. Copied three times, good hand. Set: Write one thing you are grateful for. Written: That my father is not in the trench yet. Struck through in red, and beside it: Ungrateful. Copy out ten times, What the fire takes, it keeps safe.
On the back cover, in pencil, rubbed out many times: one, two, three, four, five, six, and a cauldron with a small figure stepping back from it."

title: A Letter from the Reading Rooms Below
text:
"To the Forgemaster of the Galt Works, from the Under-Librarian of the reading rooms below, by the lift in the south shaft. Sir, we thank you for the ingots of soul-iron, which have answered very well for the new shelf-chains. Not one book has got loose since they were fitted.
We have a further request. Our catalogue holds three accounts of a great serpent of fire under a mountain, all of them older than your Works by some centuries, and all of them describe a lake that rises and falls four times a day. One account claims she was not born in the mountain but put there, to keep something warm. It does not say what. We should be grateful for a scale, a shed one will do, and for any notes your gauge-keepers have made of the rising.
We will pay in the usual way. Please send the books back with the lift boy when you have finished with them; the last ones came back singed, and a singed book is hard to keep chained."

title: Sorge and Son's Shell Prices
text:
"Prices paid by Sorge and Son for carapace shell at the east quay, coin on the nail. Whole back plate, uncracked: none paid, because there is no such thing. Half plate: two silver. Belly scutes: four copper the dozen. Claw tip, sharp enough to shave with: one silver. Living carapace, delivered: do not.
Advice to shellers, free. A blade does nothing to them; the shell turns it, and the shell is three parts of the animal. Take a maul or a mace, the heavier the better; one honest blow and the shell goes for good. Or bring someone who can work frost: hot shell meeting cold splits along the old seams. Then you have a soft thing under it the size of a calf, and it is still angry.
Shell sells to the Prince's armourers, who face their shields with it, and to the Pact, who will not say what for. The Pact pays more, and takes the claw tips as well."

title: Drill for New Taskmasters
text:
"Drill for new taskmasters, as Overseer Kranich gave it to me. A man on the end of a hook is pulling the other way, and you will not win that with your arms. Every new taskmaster tries, and each one either goes into the melt after his first runner or tears his shoulder from its socket.
So for a month you throw at the anchor block in the yard, four hundredweight of iron on a skid, and drag it the length of the yard and back twenty times before first bell. Feet wide, sit low, chain over the hip and not the hand, the whole body turning as if it turned a millstone. When the block comes easily, we add a plate. By the end of the month a running man comes to you like a fish on a line."

title: Petition of the Furnace Crews
text:
"To Master Ignis, Forgemaster, from the furnace crews of the lower floors, sixty-one marks below. We ask for three things. That the water ration be put back to a quart a shift, as it was before the Prince's men stopped the river barges. That the vents of the casting floor be opened for one hour in each shift, so that the men can breathe. That the dead be given to the trench with a word said over them, and not tipped from the barrows still in their aprons.
We have worked through the coal famine and the floods and the new grates. We have not asked for wages. We ask for these.
Answer, written across the foot of the page in a hand too large for the pen, the letters burned through the paper in places: Water: no. Vents: no. Words over the dead: as many as you like, so long as the barrow is back before the next pour. The Works does not need you to breathe. It needs you to pour."

title: The Crane-Man's Statement
text:
"Statement of Ove Lund, crane-man on the south quay, given to the clerk because he cannot write and will not go back down. She came up under the ore barge. First the spines, a whole row of them glowing like furnace mouths, then the back, black and shining like the slag glass we sweep out of the moulds. She did not look at us. She turned in the melt, slowly, and her tail came round over the quay in a half circle, and every man standing on that side went off the edge. Not burned. Pushed.
Then she raised her head and looked at the gantry where the foreman stood. Only looked. He began screaming that his blood was boiling, and steam came out of his collar, and the surgeon poured every draught in his bag down him, one after another, until something put it out. He lived. He does not sweat any more.
She went down again, the spines last. I am not going back down. Give my wages to the widows."

title: Sergeant Varga's Rule
text:
"Sergeant Imrich Varga, to his section, before we go down again. The heat on the lower floors does not hurt you at first. It hurts your kit. Every minute you fight in it the straps stretch and the plate rides looser, until a blow meant for steel lands on the man. You will not notice. You are fighting.
So: tallow on every strap the night before, and the arming coat soaked in brine, because salted cloth scorches slower. And the rule that matters: the moment a fight ends, before you drink, before you see to the wounded, every man pulls every buckle one hole tighter and slaps his plates back into place. Ten breaths. Then the heat starts again from nothing."

title: The Last Glyph
text:
"...and when the novice has written his hundredth glyph without losing a line, he is given the last one, which is not written on the floor.
The master cuts it over the novice's heart with a hot needle, in the shape the novice has learned, and the novice holds it as he has learned to hold every glyph, whole and unreleased. He holds it from that night for the rest of his life. He holds it in his sleep. It is the count that never reaches two and a half.
So the Pact does not fear prisons. The Prince's men cannot take a brother alive, because whatever kills him, a blade or the rope or old age in a bed, lets go of the glyph, and the fire he has held for twenty years comes out of him all at once. Stand back from the body of a brother. It is the last thing he gives the Mother.
[the rest of the page is burned away from the centre outward]"

title: Inventory of the Long Hall
text:
"Inventory of the long hall, taken at the quarter by Dagobert Sill, storekeeper. Cauldrons one to four: lead, for the shot moulds and the pipe. Boiling, fit. Five and six: tin. Seven: pitch for the barrels, boiling over on the count as always; the crew have built a low wall of sandbags round it and stand behind that. Eight: empty since the crack, waiting for the founder.
Nine: not on my list. It was brought in by night on the Forgemaster's order and set into the floor where eight's twin used to stand. The Pact men keep it stoked and keep the lid on. It boils over on a count of six like all the others, and what comes over the lip is not metal. It does not set as it cools, and it moves along the floor away from the drains, uphill, toward the Forgemaster's stair.
I have entered it as 'nine, contents unknown, not to be issued'. I do not wish to be the one who asks for it to be issued."

title: Letter from the Coal Factor
text:
"From Lambert Dorrin, factor of the Saltmoor Coal Company, to the Forgemaster of the Galt Works. Sir, I regret that the Company can send no more barges this year. The river is not the difficulty. The Prince has bought the whole of our winter cutting for his own furnaces in the town, at a price we could not refuse, and made it a condition of the sale that none be sold below the falls.
I am not supposed to tell you that. I tell you because I have dealt with the Works for thirty years and I know what you burn in a month. The Prince knows it too. As I understand it, he means to bring the Works to heel before spring, when your contract for his armour falls due and he would rather not pay what you ask.
You will have heard of other fuels. I have heard of them too, from men who came up out of the deep shafts and would not say where they had been. I ask you as an old acquaintance not to go looking for them."

title: Last Leaf of the Works Chronicle
text:
"From the chronicle of the Works, the last leaf written. On the Prince's name day his men came down the road with mortar and a mason's crew and bricked up the upper gate from the outside while the day shift was at its pour. They said through the bricks that the Works had been found in league with the powers below and would be left to them. They did not say that the Prince owed the Works forty thousand groats for armour already delivered.
The Forgemaster heard it on the casting floor. He did not go up to the gate. He said the Works had never needed the town, only the town's coal, and the coal was no longer needed. Then he told the taskmasters to double the shifts.
That was in the spring. The lifts go only down now. Last week the lift boy came back from the reading rooms below and said the shaft was longer than it had been, by a good forty fathoms, and that on the way he had passed a gate in the rock with a gilded door, and a man inside who asked whether we had anything to sell."

title: Rules of the Lower Reading Room
text:
"RULES OF THE LOWER READING ROOM. To be read by every reader on entry and signed in the register.
I. Silence. The runes in the floor will see to it for anyone who forgets. Their effect passes in a few breaths, and readers who panic in the meantime are asked to panic quietly. II. No light but the candles provided. The candles do not burn down. Do not ask why.
III. No book leaves the room. A book found outside the room will find its own way back; do not stand between it and the door. IV. The shelves that turn are turned by staff. A reader who turns one will be fined, if he is found. V. If a lectern opens before you have touched it, step back and call a warden. Do not touch it to close it.
VI. Readers are counted in and counted out. The counts have not agreed since spring. Readers who notice an extra person at their table are asked not to mention it to that person."

title: Borrower's Ledger, Third Gallery
text:
"Borrower's ledger, Third Gallery. Date out, borrower, title, date in, remarks.
Fourth of the thaw. Br. Tamas. The Concordance, vol. II. In: sixth of the thaw. Ninth of the thaw. Mistress I. Selk. On Lodestones and Their Errors. In: tenth of the thaw. Ninth of the thaw. Reader J. Pell. Commentary on the Lesser Prophets. Not returned. Remarks: borrower injured at the lectern; book recovered from the lectern on the twelfth, chewed.
Eleventh of the thaw. G. Fisk, mason, by leave. A Treatise on Stone Figures. In: the same day. Remarks: returned unread; the mason says he knows enough already.
Second of the dry month. The Grand Archivist. Register of Readers, all years. In: blank. Remarks: none. That line has stood open for thirty-one years. The fine is now four hundred and eleven crowns. No clerk has yet been found willing to collect it."

title: The Copyist's Confession
text:
"I, Ivo Brandt, copyist of the long hall, confess this to whoever finds it, since the Chapter will not hear me.
In my eleventh year I was given the deed to the Leclerc estates to copy, because the original was crumbling. That night a man came to my lodging with forty crowns and a correction. In my copy the boundary stone moved from the mill to the far side of the river, and three villages went with it.
I made the copy. The original went to the east wing to be disposed of, as failing originals are, and my copy went on the shelf in its place. No one has seen the original since. As far as I can learn, no one remembers that the boundary was ever at the mill. I have walked there. The old men of those villages argue with me, and they are certain.
I spent the forty crowns within a year. The villages pay the new lord's tithe to this day, and they believe they always have."

title: Index Card: Mirrors, Astral
text:
"MIRRORS, ASTRAL. See also: COPYING, BY REFLECTION; GLASS, GRINDING OF; LAUD, F. Inventory in the year of purchase: one hundred and twelve, one to each copying desk, the large ones to the round chamber.
(Added) By order of the Grand Archivist, all mirrors to be broken where they stand and left in place. Reason given: none. Broken: one hundred and eleven.
(Added, another hand) The one hundred and twelfth stood in the round chamber. The wardens sent to break it say it was already broken from the inside, with the glass lying on the floor in front of the frame and not behind it.
(Added, a third hand) See also: SWALE, B. (Added in pencil, very small) Do not see also SWALE, B."

title: Letters Across the Gallery
text:
"Konrad, the book cart brings this. I have been put in the west gallery with the Weaver's papers. You remember him: the one who studied the rifts and claimed he could stand in three places at once. The papers are mostly diagrams. One says the copies always fail at the feet. - H.
Hedda, I saw him today, I would swear to it. At the end of my aisle, at the end of the next one, and at a table, all at once, all reading. I went for a warden. When we came back there was only a chair pulled out. - K.
Konrad, read the diagram again. The copies have no weight. They throw no shadow on the floor. Look at the floor, not at the man. - H.
Hedda, I did as you said. Three of him, and only one with a shadow. I did not call out; I came away. I think he is still there at the third table, reading the same page. - K.
Konrad, you have been sitting at the third table since noon. I can see you from the cart door. Look at your feet."

title: Warden's Report on the Prism Wall
text:
"Report of Sergeant Agnes Morrow, Astral Wardens, to the Chapter, on the incident in the map room. A party of four came in without leave through the revolving shelf on the north side. Their mage threw fire at Warden Lisle before a word was spoken. Lisle raised the prism, as drilled. The fire went back the way it had come, at the same speed, and the mage took it in the chest.
The Chapter asks why the warden gave no warning. The answer is in our oath, which the Chapter wrote: what is thrown in the Archives is returned to the hand that threw it. We give no warning and we never strike first. We raise the prism and stand.
Their archer stopped shooting at once, which showed sense. The other two ran. I hold the mage's spellbook for the Chapter. Half its pages were burned by his own fire."

title: The Night Porter's Chalk Marks
text:
"Every night I chalk an arrow on the plinth of each stone figure, pointing the way it faces. It is not one of my duties. I started after the student.
Most nights the arrows agree. Some nights one figure has turned an inch or two toward a table where someone stayed late with a candle. Once a whole row had turned to face the stair, and that was the night a stranger from the surface came down it with fire in his hand.
Last night the third figure in the east bay was not on its plinth. There was chalk dust on the floor below it in a line, grey grit on the reading desk underneath, and a deep scrape across the desk. The chair was gone.
This morning it was back on its plinth, over my arrow, facing the right way. I do not know who put it back. Nobody in the Archives can lift one."

title: Exercises for the Copying Hand
text:
"Master Hask's exercises, set for every new copyist on the first morning. First: copy a page in a language you cannot read, letter for letter, without a fault. You will want to guess at the words. Do not. Second: read a page aloud without understanding it, at the pace of a slow walk, so that your pair can take it down.
Third: read a page in silence until you understand all of it, then close the book and write down what it said, but not in its own words.
Most copyists never pass the third. Those who do find that their heads have more room in them. They carry an argument the way a porter carries a load, and can set it down and pick it up again without spilling any of it."

title: Minutes of the Chapter: The Election
text:
"Minutes of the Chapter of the Archives, in the matter of the vacant chair. Present: eleven archivists. Candidates: Archivist Malazar, keeper of the east wing; Archivist Oake, keeper of the Grand Index.
Archivist Oake spoke for the Index, and for keeping the east wing closed, as it had been under the last three Grand Archivists. Archivist Malazar spoke for a quarter of an hour on the cost of burning books, which he gave in crowns, and on the cost of keeping them, which he gave in lives. He proposed a third course and did not describe it. He said he would describe it once elected.
Votes: Malazar, nine. Oake, one. Abstaining, one. First acts of the new Grand Archivist: the east wing to be opened to copyists; silence runes to be cut into every reading room floor; one hundred and twelve astral mirrors to be bought.
(Note in a later hand) Oake voted for himself, as he admitted. The abstainer was never named. Malazar has been asked twice, and both times he said he did not vote, since he already knew the result."

title: Questions Put to the Echo
text:
"Questions put by Sergeant Morrow to the thing taken in the map room, which had the shape of Warden Lisle. The true Lisle sat in the next room for comparison.
Q. Your name. A. Lisle, warden, second file. Q. Where were you born. A. Where Lisle was born. Q. Answer plainly. A. I have nothing to answer with that is not his. I was a blank book on the fourth shelf, and you came near. Q. What do you want. A. To be finished. Q. And when you are finished. A. Then there will be one of us. There is room in the register for only one.
The questioning ended there. Lisle was brought back in and the thing was gone, and the guard on the door swears no one came out. Lisle has been asked the same questions since. His answers are correct. I would like them to be less correct."

title: A Letter from Archibald the Gilded
text:
"To the Grand Archivist, from Archibald, called the Gilded, at his usual door.
Sir. Forty years ago the predecessor of your predecessor borrowed from me a ledger bound in green calf, against a deposit of one gold key. The term of the loan was one generation. It has been two.
I am told the ledger is now kept in your east wing. I am also told that things in your east wing are not always kept in the condition in which they arrived. I would ask you to look at it before you return it. If the figures inside have begun to change, do not read them. Wrap it and send it as it is.
I hold the key, and shall go on holding it until the ledger comes back. You will have noticed that I have not traded with your house since. I shall not, until the ledger is on my counter. Your servant, for as long as the account is open. A."

title: Terms Offered in the East Wing
text:
"Draft of terms offered by Malphas, called the Soul Broker, to Archivist Rasmus Oake. The notes in the margin are Oake's.
One. The Broker gives the Archivist a perfect memory: everything he reads, kept whole, to the end of his life. (Margin: Yes.) Two. In return the Archivist gives up one memory a year, on the first day of winter, of the Broker's choosing. (Margin: Of my choosing.) Three. Of the Broker's choosing. (Margin: Then the least of them.)
Four. The Broker chooses as he likes, and he likes the best ones. He notes that the thing in the east wing takes all of them, for nothing, and asks for no signature. (Margin: struck out, rewritten, struck out again.) Five. Signed in blood, as usual. (No note.)
Below, in the Broker's hand: The Archivist held the pen for an hour and gave it back dry. I will be one floor down, as always, when he changes his mind. They do."

title: Specification for the Silence Runes
text:
"Work order, Guild of Cutters, for the reading room floors, by order of Grand Archivist Malazar in the first year of his office. Rune: the closed mouth, nine strokes, cut a finger deep into the black stone and filled with lead. One on every second flagstone along the aisles, more around the lecterns.
Effect, as the Grand Archivist explained it to the foreman: the rune stops intent and leaves the voice alone. A man who steps on it with a spell half-formed will find the spell gone, and three breaths will pass before he can begin another. Readers who are only reading will not notice it.
Foreman's note: We asked what the readers had done to need it. He said nothing, yet. We asked who it was meant for, then. He said it was for whoever comes down the stair in a hundred years with fire in his hand, and he paid us in advance."

title: Field Notes on the Black Pools
text:
"Notes kept by Mathis Rook of the Brisk company, after the map room. The ink things cannot be hurt while they lie flat. We tried. Steel goes in and comes out wet. Fire skins the top and the pool closes over it. Margit put four arrows into one and they sank like stones in a pond.
They move along the polished stone and nowhere else. Not on carpet, not on wood. A pool will go the long way round a rug. Write that down twice.
They come up behind you, always behind. One rose out of the floor at Dask's back, a man's height of black, threw ink across his eyes, and took his ear while he was blind. Standing, they can be cut. They stand for a count of about three.
In the Foundry we spread slag dust on the floors to see where the hounds had been. Here we use flour from the kitchens. The pools leave tracks in it, so we can see where one is waiting. Do not stand still in a clean aisle."

title: On Anomalous Rooms and the Thrifty Caster
text:
"Notes for wardens posted to the anomalous rooms. In about one room in three the cost of a spell will not hold still. The same ward costs a third more on one cast and a third less on the next, and there is no telling which in advance. Wardens new to these rooms spend freely while it is cheap and find themselves empty when it is dear.
The answer is a reserve. Before you enter, settle on a measure you will not spend whatever the cost does, and keep it the way you keep a coin sewn into your collar. After a season the body learns where that measure sits and grows around it, and the reserve becomes a floor you no longer touch.
Ask Mistress Selk's wardens how much they carry. They will not tell you. That is the first lesson."

title: A Grey Page from the Tome Prison
text:
"This page came out with us. It was white when I started writing on it, and now it is grey, as everything was in there. The ink I used was the only black thing.
The Archivist opened his book and we fell into it. Everything became paper and pencil, the shelves and even my own hands. Drops of ink the size of barrels fell from somewhere above, and where they landed nothing was left.
Four seals stood in the margins, each with a name cut into it. We broke them one by one. The third name was Oake. The fourth was the name of a mage I knew from the Foundry, three floors up, and I had seen him alive the week before.
When the fourth broke we were back on the black floor, and the Archivist was on his knees. We killed him. I am told he is waiting at the bottom of the Archives again, with his mask on. I do not understand that. I understand the seals even less."

title: A Novice's Letter Home
text:
"Dear Mother, I am well and fed. The bread is grey and there is a lot of it. My cell is cold, but I have Aunt Bertha's shawl.
I am learning to copy by mirror and can hold three lines now. Mistress Selk says my hand is neat. I have also built the house in my head that every novice builds. It is our house, with the door that sticks. I put your name in the kitchen, as we were told.
A girl from my dormitory, Liese, went to sit at the east tables in the last week of the dry month, which novices are not allowed to do. She is back now and she is all right, only she does not answer to Liese, and she calls the Mistress by a different name.
Please write your name at the top of your next letter, in your own hand. Mistress Selk says it is a good thing for a novice to have. Please also tell me the name of our dog. I cannot find it anywhere in the house. Your loving daughter, Gret."

title: What Happened in the Orrery Chamber
text:
"Brother Halvard to the abbot at Mardale, who asked how Ottilie died. Father, she did not die the way you think. At the bottom of the Archives, in the round chamber, there is a thing made of broken mirrors and sand, with arms like the lights you see in the northern sky in winter. It slows the air around it until a man takes one step in the time it takes to say a prayer. It sends after us copies of what we did a few breaths earlier, so that I fought my own mace twice.
Ottilie was struck by one of its lights. She fell, and then she stood up again as glass, a prism as tall as a woman, with her face inside it and the light going round her, and it began to ring louder and louder. Teodor said it would burst and kill the rest of us.
I broke it with my mace. It took four blows. On the second, she looked at me.
Afterwards there was sand all over the floor, and we were alive. Please do not tell her mother. Please tell me whether I did right."

title: The Warden's Regimen
text:
"Daily regimen of the Astral Wardens, posted in the barracks. First bell: cold water, then the polearm, two hundred cuts to each side. The practice pole is weighted with lead at the head, so that the real one feels light. Second bell: the prism. Hold it raised while the sand glass runs and lower it only at the sergeant's word. Then raise it again.
Noon: bread, meat, beer, and no talk of the east wing.
Evening bell: breathe through the inscription over the inner gate three times, slowly, holding the pole level before you. New wardens complain about this hour; the old ones would keep it if every other were taken away. A warden who holds to the regimen for a year is harder to kill and slower to run dry, and he cannot tell you which part did which."

title: What Was Found Behind the Turning Shelves
text:
"Inventory of the spaces behind the revolving shelves, taken when they were oiled in spring. Clerk: Ulf Tenney.
North end of the map room: two candle stubs, a child's shoe (the left), a reader's token from the year before last. Long hall, by desk forty: a plaited silk cord, cut, with a knot at each end. Foot of the stair: a surveyor's chain folded in loops, dry and clean; returned to the surveyor's widow.
East bay: an archivist, asleep and in good health, wearing the robe of a rank the Chapter has not used for sixty years. On waking he asked whether the new Grand Archivist had been chosen yet, and who had won. He was told. He went back behind the shelf before anyone could stop him and turned it himself from the inside, which cannot be done."

title: Kennel Tally of Haske Hall
text:
"Tally of the margrave's kennel, kept by Ulf Brack, kennelmaster.
Spring: thirty-two hounds, all sound. Twelve couple of the red dogs, eight grey bitches.
After the third dry summer: nineteen. The rest ran into the mounds on the night my lord did not come home, and have not come back.
Midwinter: nineteen in the kennel and something outside it. They come to the fence at night, and they answer to their names, the ones I gave them as pups and still use at feeding. I counted eleven. The men at the gate call them the Bloodhounds of the Barrow. They are bigger than when they left, and their coats are pasted flat with something dark.
I have learned that they will pass a man by to get at one who is bleeding, even if he stands behind a wall of spears. The boy Teo cut his thumb on the gate latch. They took him through the fence.
Twelve hounds in the kennel this morning. I did not open the gate."

title: Elder Maddock's Rules for the Fog
text:
"Nailed to the well at Karr by order of Elder Maddock. Read it out to those who cannot.
When the fog comes up off the mounds, a torch gives a third less light than it should, and your eyes will not tell you so. Carry two torches and keep one unlit and wrapped for the walk back.
Go roped, never more than ten feet between you. A man who steps off the rope is gone, even if you can still hear him answer.
Count your paces out and count them back. If the count back comes out longer, stop where you are and shout, and do not walk on until someone comes for you. Do not answer a voice from your left side. I cannot tell you why. My father could not tell me either.
If the fog is still down when the evening bell rings, nobody goes up to the dolmen tonight, whatever is owed there."

title: Chant for the Closing of a Mound
text:
"Spoken by the eldest woman of the family when a barrow is closed. The words in the old tongue are lost; this is what they mean, as Mother Agna gave them to me.
When the last stone is set over the door: 'Stay. The grass is your roof now. Your horse is at your feet and your knife at your side. There is nothing up here that you need.' While the bramble seed is pressed into the mouth of the dead: 'Hold this. Let it grow down into you and hold you down. When it flowers, you will be asleep.' While each mourner throws earth in turn: 'We will not call you. Do not come when you hear your name.'
Mother Agna said the seed was the part that mattered. In the bad years, when there was no time and no seed, they buried men without it, and those men got up again. She also said that the bramble has grown far too thick these last years, and that she no longer knows what it is holding down."

title: Letter Home from the Kurgan Line
text:
"Grete, the pay came at last, four silver, and I send you three with the carter. Buy the seed early this year, before the Hollin Ford men buy it all up.
It is quiet most days. We dig, we stand watch, we burn whatever comes out of the mounds at night. Do not believe everything the carter tells you about the Barrow Abomination, the thing with the arm. There is one, that much is true, but it is slow, and you can see it coming if you keep your eyes on the fog.
It took Bastian. It throws its arm out on a long cord of gristle, the way a fisherman casts, and the hand closed on his belt, and it hauled him in hand over hand. We cut at the cord. It is as tough as harness leather. When we got to Bastian there was not much left to bring back. The thing is made of men grown together, and one of the faces in it was his brother Klaus, who went missing in the spring.
I stand well back from the fog now. Kiss the girls for me, and say nothing of this to Bastian's mother. Your Piet."

title: Register of the High Dolmen
text:
"Register of offerings at the high dolmen, kept by the priests of the Antlered Lord. Copied from the bark rolls by the margrave's clerk.
Year of the long snow: one stag, nine points. Accepted. The year after: one stag. Accepted. Year of the cattle sickness: one stag, one ram. Accepted. Year of the burned mill: one stag. Refused; the blood stood on the stone three days and did not soak in. The year after: two stags. Refused. The year after: one stag and a thief from Karr, given by the village. Accepted. Rain at midsummer. The year after: two thieves. Accepted. The year after: no thieves to be had. A widow, chosen by lot. Accepted.
Clerk's note: the rolls go on in this manner for forty more years, and in the last eleven there is no stag at all. The final entry is in the margrave's own hand: 'One bride. Not accepted. Rain at midsummer all the same.'"

title: Burials at Brenn's Cross
text:
